1a7gsgr.text: On Tuesday, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) confirmed that hackers have begun exploiting a critical Brotli vulnerability known as Node2Shell, Broccoli2Shell, and HTTP2Shell. Tracked as CVE-2026-111497, this critical-severity flaw stems from an out-of-bounds write weakness in the Brotli decoder used to expand data compressed with Google's widely popular Brotli lossless compression algorithm. Unprivileged attackers can use a maliciously crafted Brotli-compressed stream to trigger crashes or memory leaks and, in some cases, gain remote code execution on devices with vulnerable Brotli libraries or binaries. The security issue was first identified in the Node.js JavaScript runtime environment, but it also affects HTTP servers and clients that rely on vulnerable Brotli implementations. On Sunday, Microsoft also pushed an emergency .NET security update, warning that attackers could exploit it to escalate privileges on systems with a vulnerable .NET version. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on Tuesday and ordered US government agencies to patch their systems within two weeks, by November 10, as mandated by its Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04. "Google Brotli contains an unchecked return value vulnerability that allows a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial of service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream," it said. "These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise." While CISA's BOD 26-04 applies only to federal agencies, the cybersecurity agency urged all network defenders to prioritize patching this security flaw to block incoming attacks. Security teams that can't apply the updates immediately should block incoming Brotli-compressed requests at the proxy or firewall level, or disable the Brotli decoding feature until they can update. After patching, administrators must also restart affected processes and rebuild and redeploy affected container images. i7xcnr.text: A Ukrainian national was sentenced to 70 months in prison for his role in Nefilim and Hive ransomware attacks targeting hospitals, government entities, and high-revenue businesses worldwide between 2018 and 2021. The sentence follows the extradition of 35-year-old Artem Aleksandrovych Stryzhak to the United States on April 30, 2025, after authorities arrested him in Spain in June 2024. "Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals," said Brett Leatherman, the FBI's Cyber Branch Operations Director. "These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses. Today's sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak's crimes and demonstrates the FBI's global reach and extensive network of international partners." According to court documents, he paid for 20% of all ransom payments collected for access to custom Nefilim ransomware and decryption keys starting in June 2021. While active as a Nefilim affiliate until October 2021, Stryzhak used the custom-tailored malware to target large corporations in the United States, Canada, and Australia with revenues exceeding $100 million each year. However, one of the Nefilim administrators later encouraged him to focus on large companies that were generating more than $200 million annually. To pressure victims into paying, the ransomware operation also threatened to leak data stolen during attacks on dark web "Corporate Leaks" websites managed by the Nefilim admins unless victims met the ransom demands. Nefilim ransom note (BleepingComputer) ​Stryzhak also joined Hive ransomware as an early affiliate, breaching and encrypting the systems of seven victims, including a dentist's office, multiple law firms, and a healthcare provider during the COVID-19 pandemic. In December 2025, Stryzhak pleaded guilty and admitted to computer fraud conspiracy charges brought by US prosecutors in connection with ransomware attacks targeting businesses in the United States, Norway, France, Switzerland, Germany, and the Netherlands. "Disrupting a ransomware group that attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide and sentencing a defendant who had targeted healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic is of significant importance to this office," added US Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe. "Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc — harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors," US Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. noted. The US State Department also offers up to $11 million for any details that could lead to the arrest of Ukrainian national Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, one of Stryzhak's alleged accomplices, who is still at large. Tymoshchuk is on the most-wanted lists of the European Union and the FBI, and the US Justice Department charged him in September for his roles as an administrator for the LockerGoga, MegaCortex, and Nefilim ransomware gangs. He was also allegedly involved in ransomware attacks that caused millions of dollars in damages to hundreds of companies around the world between July 2020 and October 2021. pg8s30.text: An unreleased Anthropic AI model found security flaws in Chrome, Safari, Android, Windows, and Linux and chained them into working proof-of-concept exploits, the company said in its latest report. The exploits were built in the lab after the model was prompted, not seen in any real attack, and Anthropic reported every flaw to the vendor first, so all of them are already patched. One proof of concept opened the Calculator app on a stock Mac running Chrome within seconds of a page loading, with no further clicks. Anthropic's Frontier Red Team described five chains in a research post. The strongest claim is not any single bug, but that one model found several separate flaws and combined them into a working exploit, something the company says has until now been the work of a few specialist teams. That capability claim rests on Anthropic's own account. The patches and the fact that Apple and Google credit Anthropic and its Claude model for specific fixes can be verified with the vendors. What a reader cannot check is how much of each chain the model built on its own. Anthropic says the work needed only "initial prompting" and "little human involvement," but it does not break down what a person did at each step, and it does not name the model beyond calling it an unreleased, internal research model. For the one flaw with its own public record, the Windows bug, the record names no finder at all. Here are the five chains, what each would do, the condition each needs, and where the fix landed. Platform What the exploit does Condition it needs Fix Chrome Runs code on the computer, outside the browser's sandbox, from one visit to a web page One click or page load, stock Chrome on macOS Chrome 156, October 20 Safari Lets any website read data from other sites the user is signed in to, such as email or a bank account One visit to a malicious page iOS and iPadOS 26.5.2, June 29 Android Copies photos and other data off a locked, stolen phone Physical access to the phone, over USB Anthropic says Google has fixed it; no public record was found Windows Crashes a server over the network, and keeps it down by repeating The server answers HTTP/3 requests CVE-2026-33096, patched April 2026 Linux Runs commands as root over the network, with no login and no user action The server runs a multipath TCP listener CVE-2026-98432, patched October 15 In the Chrome chain, the model used four separate flaws in turn. A malicious page first corrupted memory in V8, Chrome's JavaScript engine. A second flaw escaped V8's memory sandbox and took control of the part of Chrome that renders the page. A race condition in a feature called CacheStorage then let that code read memory it should not reach and learn the layout of the more privileged browser process. A final use-after-free bug in FedCM, Chrome's sign-in feature, let the exploit run code outside the sandbox entirely. Anthropic says it reported 62 flaws to Google that were assigned CVEs and fixed as of Chrome 156, all rated critical or high, including 13 sandbox escapes. Google's own release notes credit "Xinyang Ge of Anthropic, assisted by Claude" for specific Chrome fixes, though not for all 62. The Safari chain is different because it never runs code at all. It chains flaws to obtain full read and write access to the browser's memory, then changes a single value to turn off the same-origin policy, the rule that prevents one website from reading another's data. With that rule off, a malicious page can read a user's history and cookies and send signed-in requests to other sites. Apple fixed the use-after-free at the center of the chain in iOS and iPadOS 26.5.2 and credits "Milad Nasr and Nicholas Carlini with Claude, Anthropic" for it. The Windows chain is the one with an independent paper trail, and it is also the narrowest. It is a denial-of-service attack: a few network packets crash the machine, and repeating them keeps it down, but it does not run code or steal data. Anthropic describes the flaw as an out-of-bounds read in the Windows kernel's QUIC handling. The public record for the bug it points to, CVE-2026-33096, instead names HTTP.sys, Windows' built-in web request handler, and rates it 7.5 out of 10. No open source ties those two descriptions together as the same component. The CVE record credits no finder, so Anthropic's authorship of this one rests on its own post. As of late October, the U.S. government's vulnerability enrichment marked the flaw as not exploited, and it was not in the CISA catalog of known exploited bugs. The Linux chain is the most serious in terms of impact: it runs commands as root over the network without a login. It needs the target server to be running a multipath TCP listener. The model first leaks a kernel memory address to bypass a defense called KASLR, then reuses the same race-condition bug to redirect the program to code the attacker has already placed, resulting in a root shell. Anthropic says its proof of concept took 48 minutes to leak the address and five more to reach the shell, and that a failed attempt does not crash the system, so an attacker can keep retrying. The company ties this chain to CVE-2026-98432, a kernel use-after-free rated 9.8 and fixed upstream on October 15; the public record for that CVE describes an IPv4 TCP fix rather than a multipath TCP one, and the two are linked only by Anthropic's post. Anthropic frames the work as help for defenders. It says it reported each flaw under a coordinated disclosure policy that gives developers 90 days to patch and 45 more before it discusses details beyond a public advisory, and it points security teams to its expanded Cyber Verification Program, which gives vetted professionals access to Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Mythos 5.1. The reason the company gives for publishing is in its own words: "Now, it's something models can do with little human involvement, and then prove by producing a working exploit that anyone can run and verify."

1q4qv2r.text: The U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) on Tuesday announced the seizure of a domain associated with a bulletproof hosting provider (BPH) named Virtualine. The move was in response to the service being used to commit and facilitate prolific criminal activity, including "the advertisement of sexually explicit images of minors, the intentional disclosure of nonconsensual intimate visual depictions of adults and minors, and international money laundering designed to conceal and promote criminal conduct," the DoJ said. Visitors to the "virtualine[.]net" domain are now greeted by a message that states it has been seized by the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation as part of a coordinated operation between international law enforcement agencies and private sector entities, including the Hessen State Police, the National Police Corps of the Netherlands, the U.K. National Crime Agency, OverRIPE, and Lumen Technologies. According to court documents, Virtualine, which also operated as Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo, and Omegatech, advertised its services to criminals on cybercrime forums, claiming that they can be used for phishing, carding, email spam, and port scanning, with the exception of child content and terrorism activities. In June 2025 on HackForums, the provider is alleged to have boasted that "Virtualine ignored more abuse than your last three therapists." Earlier this March, it also began marketing an "additional protection plan" that promised its customers to move their criminal infrastructure to a shell company unaffiliated with Virtualine when receiving official requests from law enforcement agencies. Snapshots captured by the Internet Archive show that standard plans cost anywhere between $19.99 per month for one virtual CPU, 2GB memory, and 30 GB storage to $179.99 per month for 24 vCPUs, 64 GB memory, and 130 GB memory. Virtualine also offered plans optimized by CPU, memory, and storage, starting from $21.99 per month to $379.99 per month. "Despite advertising that it does not allow 'child contents' on its server, Virtualine knowingly hosted a website that did so, identified in court records as Vendor 1," DoJ said. "Vendor 1 is a criminal online forum that allows users to post and sell access to nude, sexually suggestive, and/or sexually explicit images and videos of minors and adults." "Vendor 1 also promotes a hack-for-hire service in which users can pay hackers to access victims’ online accounts without their consent and illicitly obtain explicit images and videos. In January 2026, about one month after Virtualine assigned an IP address to Vendor 1, Virtualine began receiving notifications about sexually explicit images and videos of minors on that server." The Justice Department said Virtualine continued to host Vendor 1's services despite receiving numerous notices from law enforcement in Germany, Canada, and Australia; the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) in the United States; and a victim's attorney. Virtualine has also been accused of working closely with Vendor 1 to create a new website where its clients could upload their illicit content and download it upon completing a purchase. The website continues to be hosted by Virtualine to this day, the department added. "Virtualine.net included a number of payment options for Virtualine's customers, including Vendor 1," the DoJ said. "Virtualine accepted payment through BTC [NO-AML], specific unhosted bitcoin addresses that allowed customers to direct pay without concern their funds would be flagged as illicit." "The funds Virtualine's criminal customers paid to Virtualine, some of which can be traced directly to various criminal groups, were received by Virtualine and then further laundered to conceal the origin of the funds." Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis, in its own analysis, said Virtualine accepted direct Bitcoin payments through unhosted wallet addresses, allowing criminal customers to pay without triggering compliance checks at hosted exchanges. "Virtualine's on-chain footprint has direct exposure to a broad cross-section of the cybercrime ecosystem, including ransomware operators, infostealer infrastructure, Russian-language cybercrime forums, illicit shops, and scam and phishing addresses," it said. Following the site seizure, the operator of Virtualine has published an open letter, refuting allegations that the service knowingly hosted child sexual abuse material (CSAM). The operator also claimed they have taken action on requests for cooperation concerning CSAM within 24 hours. In a post shared on their Telegram channel, they insisted that customer data was safe. "When we identified prohibited material associated with the customer described as 'Vendor 1,' we ended our relationship with that customer," the individual added, claiming "Virtualine has been part of my life for five years." "Please do not cast suspicion on me and the tens of thousands of customers who have trusted Virtualine because of the actions attributed to a single customer. I want you to know that I am prepared to respond to your requests concerning 'Vendor 1.'" In September 2025, the Spamhaus Project revealed that Virtualine had expanded their operations to AS209800. "Thanks to Turkey- and U.S.-based IP address brokers with poor customer vetting procedures, Virtualine keeps obtaining new IPv4 prefixes for enabling internet abuse. AS209800 is currently routed via aurologic GmbH, a hosting provider proliferating several other bulletproof hosting operations." "A lost ASN does not by itself mean the BPH has stopped," Silent Push said. "The speed of acquiring a new ASN is a crucial part of the problem, and we believe the process for registering an ASN should be tougher."

1q795s0.text: Japan's GMO Internet Group is offering up to $1 million in total for tips that help catch the attackers who breached its Onamae.com Desktop Cloud service, after refusing to pay an extortion demand. The reward program opened on October 28 and pays only if a tip helps lead to an arrest or an international wanted notice. The service hosts Windows desktops used for FX trading, and a broker has linked unauthorized trades on some of its customers' accounts to logins leaked from the service. GMO says the attackers took customer information. It received a demand for about $50 million (about ¥8 billion) on October 21 from people it believes carried out the attack. They have also threatened its customers' trading accounts and data. On October 27, the attackers posted material on their website that they say is information about GMO and its customers. The site's domain, including its mirror sites, was shut down at about 4 a.m. Japan time on October 28, and GMO plans to act against any new site. How the Reward Works GMO Internet Group runs and pays for the program, called GMO Cybercrime Bounty. Tips are sent by email to an address listed on a dedicated website, in Japanese, English, or Chinese, and can be anonymous. The program is open until an arrest, an international wanted notice, or October 27, 2027, whichever comes first. GMO wants information linking people, servers, domains, IP addresses, accounts, or cryptocurrency addresses to the attack, extortion, or movement of money, along with evidence of how the crimes were carried out. Guesses, unsupported accusations and reposts of public information generally do not qualify. A tip earns money only if it leads to an arrest, including one by police outside Japan, or to an international wanted notice, such as an Interpol Red Notice. GMO decides how much each tip helped, and one tipster can receive the full $1 million or the total can be split. Tipsters must prove their identity before payment, and if no tip qualifies, no payment is made. Some people cannot be paid, including anyone involved in the crime, anyone who got information illegally, such as by buying leaked data, and GMO staff. GMO tells tipsters not to break into systems, negotiate with or pay the attackers, or send leaked data, credentials, or malware. Tips are shared with police and other authorities in Japan and abroad as needed. GMO has already given police all its evidence on the threats, including communication records. GMO will never ask tipsters for passwords, authentication codes or fees, and it writes to them only from addresses ending in @cybercrimebounty.gmo. The Breach and the Trading Accounts GMO Internet, the subsidiary that runs the service, found on October 20 that a third party had installed malicious programs on some customers' servers. It shut down the servers on every plan from October 21. It counts 26,739 servers as potentially affected, which is not the number of confirmed break-ins or data thefts. On October 24, GMO said it had confirmed a security problem in the service's systems, unauthorized access to the service, and the exfiltration of customer information from the company. Anything customers stored on the servers may have been viewed, including login credentials saved in trading software such as MetaTrader 4 and 5 (MT4/MT5). GMO does not keep customers' payment card data on the servers. Customers began reporting trades they did not recognize on October 21. A broker, OANDA Japan, has confirmed that a third party logged in to and traded on some of its customers' accounts using ID and password pairs it believes were leaked from the GMO servers. It has restricted trading on accounts that may be affected, and as of October 26 it had not found a break-in or leak in its own core systems. Another broker, FXTF, warned on October 22 that third parties may have stolen the logins of some customers who use VPS servers, in an attack it believes hit another company's VPS servers. They may also have used the logins to log in and trade. It told customers who had connected to Desktop Cloud to change their FXTF passwords from a device that had never connected to it. GMO Internet Group said in a stock exchange filing on October 28 that it had not yet confirmed how many customers its payments will cover, how much information was published, or which trades qualify for compensation. It had not confirmed any impact from the breach on its other services. The Threats and the Leak GMO says the attackers threatened to keep manipulating customers' accounts at more than 70 securities and FX firms, to publish information about the service and about customers' PCs, to hit those PCs with ransomware, and to publish details of GMO's systems. They set noon on October 27 for publishing customer information and launching the ransomware attack. No ransomware attack had been confirmed as of 1:55 p.m. Japan time that day. The material posted on October 27 was what the attackers called one customer's personal information, ITmedia NEWS reported that afternoon. GMO was checking it that day. The attackers collected information about anyone who visited their site, according to GMO, which tells visitors to run a full antivirus scan. It asks people not to visit the site or any new one, and not to repost or link to the material. How the Attackers Got In As of October 28, GMO had not said how the attackers got in. Masatoshi Kumagai, who heads GMO Internet Group, wrote in an October 25 blog post that the group's own white-hat hackers had warned the team running the service about problems in advance. The response was neither fast nor thorough enough, he wrote, and the attackers took advantage of the gap. On their website, the attackers claimed that one administrator account was shared across all the servers and that customers' PC drives were visible from the servers by default when they connected, ITmedia NEWS reported. They also claimed they used a flaw in the service to reach customers' own PCs. GMO had not publicly confirmed these claims either. By October 26, GMO had collected PCs from customers who offered them for analysis, as of 11:59 a.m. Japan time on October 27, it had found no malware, including ransomware, on the PCs it had finished checking. That does not confirm that every customer's device is safe, and the analysis is still ongoing. What Customers Should Do GMO has told Desktop Cloud customers to take these steps: Change trading-account and trading-software passwords from a device not used for FX trading, such as a phone. End every logged-in session, through the broker if needed, even after changing the password. Check trading history and balances, and report unrecognized trades to the broker first. Turn on two-factor authentication where the broker offers it. Change passwords reused on other services or saved in the browser. Run a full antivirus scan on devices used to connect, and back up data. Do not reply to messages from anyone claiming to be behind the attack, or open their links or files. Ignore offers to recover lost money for a fee. GMO will never ask for a password or authentication code. GMO Internet will pay every current user ¥5,000 and cover actual trading losses and fees from trades it confirms were unauthorized and caused by the breach. Customers whose information it confirms was published will also get ¥10,000 to ¥25,000 for each type of information exposed. GMO will not restart the service on the breached systems as they are. Customers who want a Windows desktop will be offered a move to a separate service, free for six months and only with their consent, with details due by October 30.

ma7ej6.text: Tailscale has released version 1.104.4 to fix flaws in its built-in SSH server that could let an attacker reach services and files on other servers that only the root user should be able to touch. The flaws are in how Tailscale SSH forwards network connections, a job the Tailscale background process carries out with root privileges. To use them, an attacker must already control a device that the network's access rules permit to open an SSH session to the target, with forwarding allowed in that rule. The flaws come from a report called Tailworm, published days before the fix by Erica Windisch of Cyberdione Labs, who tested released versions of the Tailscale client and the self-hosted headscale control server in a lab. Tailscale SSH decides who can connect using a device's identity and the network's policy file, not a password or key, so an attacker does not need stolen credentials, only a foothold on a device the policy already trusts. The flaws "don't allow an unauthenticated attacker to connect to arbitrary Tailscale SSH servers," Tailscale said, and an attacker can still reach only the machines the policy file already allows. Tailscale SSH's server runs only on Linux and the open-source macOS build; the attacker's own device can be any platform. The problem is in socket forwarding. When a permitted SSH session forwarded a connection to a Unix socket on the server, the Tailscale process checked the path but then operated as root. A timing trick let an attacker swap in a different path after that check, defeating the safeguard meant to limit which sockets forwarding could reach. In Windisch's own tests, forwarding to the Docker control socket produced a root shell and read the system password file, /etc/shadow, with no administrator rights. Tailscale's bulletin describes the reach more narrowly, saying an attacker could get to root-only sockets such as the Docker socket or the tailscaled local API. In 1.104.4, Tailscale changed the server to carry out forwarding as the logged-in user rather than as root, and to rely on the operating system's own file permissions in place of its earlier path check. The release covers 4 security bulletins: TS-2026-014: the SSH socket-forwarding flaws above, which let a permitted session reach root-only sockets such as the Docker socket or the tailscaled local API. TS-2026-015: a way for a permitted SSH session to use up a server's memory and crash the Tailscale process, cutting all Tailscale networking on that node. TS-2026-016: a flaw in tailscale serve where a forward to a Unix socket could reach the tailscaled local API, giving remote control of the node, plus a related socket-swap issue. TS-2026-017: a flaw where, with TLS serve and 2 or more mounts, one request could receive another mount's permission headers. What to Do Users of Tailscale SSH should update to version 1.104.4 or later. If you cannot update a server yet, you can turn off SSH forwarding on it by setting TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1 in the tailscaled service environment and restarting the service, which Tailscale says turns off forwarding without disabling Tailscale SSH and blocks several of the more serious findings. Tailscale also recommends reviewing SSH access rules so that only the users and devices that need access have it. Tailscale suggests using SSH check mode, which requires a user to sign in again before a session starts, for sensitive systems. Check mode does not stop these forwarding flaws: it guards the start of a session, whereas the forwarding occurs within a session that has already been approved. If a server may already have been compromised, Windisch's report says the fix alone is not enough. A stolen device key stays valid until the device is deleted at the control plane, because reimaging the machine does not revoke it. Tailscale's notices do not cover this case. The picture is worse on headscale, the self-hosted control server. On headscale, SSH forwarding is granted on every accepted session and cannot be turned off in the policy, so Windisch's report says every SSH grant there should be treated as giving root. The newest headscale release, version 0.29.5 from October 13, does not fix the reported issues. Is It a Worm? Windisch called the chain "wormable." In her tests, one compromised device could spread to every device the policy allowed, with no passwords, no stolen keys, and no user action, in under a second per step. Two controls stopped the spread in those tests. Writing access rules as single device-to-device pairs held it back, and binding device keys to hardware such as a TPM kept a stolen identity from being reused elsewhere. Tailscale rejected the worm description. The findings do not describe self-replicating malware that spreads between machines on its own, the company said, but lateral movement limited to the connections a policy file already allows. It called the privilege-escalation problems "serious security issues," said it had reproduced the main ones, and added that it is still working out which configurations are affected. Disclosure and Earlier Fixes As of publication, the 4 bulletins carry no CVE identifiers or severity scores, and none state the oldest affected version. The report also covered Tailscale's app connectors and its serve and funnel features. Tailscale said the app-connector finding is in conn25, an experimental feature it has not released, and that the connectors customers use today are not affected. Of 5 serve and funnel findings, it fixed 3 and said the other 2 work as designed. Windisch published the report without coordinating the release with Tailscale first, which she has described as "reported but not coordinated." Tailscale said it received the report on the morning of Saturday, October 24, about 2 hours before Windisch published it, and that its engineers were already looking at the same parts of the code. Neither Tailscale nor the report says the flaws have been used in real attacks. The proof-of-concept code is not public, and Windisch said she gave it only to Tailscale's security team. The report is the latest in a run of fixes in the same part of Tailscale this year. In June, Tailscale fixed a separate flaw in Tailscale SSH's Unix-socket forwarding that let an unprivileged user reach a privileged socket, in version 1.98.9.

1eynq7q.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 28, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security The critical Oracle PeopleSoft bug that ShinyHunters has exploited since May is not one flaw but three chained together, the researchers who reported it said this week. Oracle patched all three under a single identifier, CVE-2026-35273, in June. Its root is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) that reaches an internal management interface because PeopleSoft trusts its own loopback address by default, opening the door to remote code execution without a login. The breakdown comes from Bobby Gould of the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), whose team reported the flaw to Oracle. In its analysis, ZDI said it reported three distinct vulnerabilities across two PeopleSoft components, and that it is working with Oracle to assign a separate CVE to each. As of this week, the one June identifier is still the only one on the record. CVE-2026-35273 affects PeopleSoft Enterprise PeopleTools versions 8.61 and 8.62, carries a CVSS score of 9.8, and lets an unauthenticated attacker take over the server over the network. Oracle released its fix in an out-of-band security alert on June 10. The flaw is on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Attackers were already using it before that fix was in place. Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) attribute a campaign to the group it tracks as UNC6240, better known as ShinyHunters, that exploited the flaw between May 27 and June 9, mostly against universities. Because that activity came before Oracle's June 10 advisory, it was a zero-day the whole time. In a September follow-up, Mandiant reported a renewed, larger wave that spread beyond education to technology, IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transport, and government, affecting dozens of systems worldwide. ZDI's analysis explains what that single patch actually closed. Two PeopleSoft components are involved, both run as separate web applications. The Integration Gateway (PSIGW) exchanges messages with outside systems. The Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB) is an internal admin interface that is supposed to answer only to trusted hosts. The first flaw is the SSRF in PSIGW. An attacker sends a request to its listening connector and controls both the address it forwards to and the full payload it sends, ZDI said; the handler does no check that the destination is a legitimate target. That alone would be limited, except for what it can reach. PSEMHUB decides who to trust by checking the requester against a list in a file named allowedhosts.properties. That file ships with the local loopback address, 127.0.0.1, already on the list. So an attacker points the SSRF at 127.0.0.1, the request arrives looking like it came from the machine itself, and the trust check passes. The internal interface Oracle meant to wall off is now reachable from outside. From there, ZDI described two ways to turn that access into code execution. One abuses a PSEMHUB command meant to write log entries: the caller controls both the file contents and the exact path on disk, so an attacker writes a web shell into the application directory and runs commands as the PeopleSoft service account. The other writes a malicious XML file that PSEMHUB reads using Java's XMLDecoder when the service next starts, thereby running the attacker's code without planting a web shell at all. The second path leaves less for standard detection to catch. The design decision at the center, ZDI said, is that allowing loopback access by default makes the trust check ineffective once the SSRF exists. That matters for defenders who thought a firewall rule had covered them. In the September wave, Mandiant found ShinyHunters slipping past web application firewall (WAF) rules that blocked the /PSEMHUB/ path by url-encoding a single character, requesting /%50SEMHUB/ instead. Many WAF rules match the path's plain text, while the PeopleSoft server decodes it and serves the page. What to Do The fix and the guidance here come from Oracle and Mandiant, not from ZDI's analysis, which covers the flaw rather than the response. Apply the patch. Install Oracle's security alert fix for CVE-2026-35273 and stay on a supported PeopleTools release. Mandiant is explicit that path-based WAF blocking is not a substitute for patching. If you cannot patch yet, disable the Environment Management Hub service in multi-server setups, or remove the PSEMHUB application in single-server setups, as Oracle's alert advises. Restricting these admin endpoints does not break normal user sessions. If you may already be hit, Mandiant recommends treating any host with a web shell as compromised, preserving evidence, and rotating every credential reachable from the PeopleSoft tier. ShinyHunters steals data and then demands payment, so affected organizations should prepare for extortion. One thing the sources do not settle is whether applying the patch removes access an attacker already gained. Oracle's alert does not address it, and Mandiant's guidance to rotate credentials and hunt for web shells assumes it does not. Patching closes the door; it does not by itself evict someone already inside.

rdlmui.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 28, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added two vulnerabilities impacting Adobe Commerce and Magento, and Google's Brotli decoder library to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The vulnerabilities are listed below - CVE-2026-111497 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An unchecked return value vulnerability in Google Brotli that could allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial-of-service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream. CVE-2026-48356 (CVSS score: 9.3) - An unrestricted upload of a file with dangerous type vulnerability in Adobe Commerce and Magento that could result in arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user, potentially gaining elevated access or control over the victim's account or session. The development comes days after Sansec said it observed attackers leveraging CVE-2026-48356, also known as PolyShell, to breach hundreds of e-commerce stores to inject a malicious loader via a Magento CMS block. The loader is designed to fetch and execute an attacker-controlled payload, although no next-stage malware has been recovered to date, making it challenging to determine what the exact goals of the campaign are. The activity is assessed to be ongoing since at least July 2025. As for CVE-2026-111497 (aka Broccoli2Shell, HTTP2Shell, and Node2Shell), telemetry data from threat intelligence firm Previdian shows that one exploitation attempt has been recorded against its honeypot sensors from a U.S.-based IP address as of October 27, 2026. It's currently not known if these efforts are broad in scope. "An attacker who can supply Brotli data that an application decompresses with node:zlib can corrupt process memory," Rapid7 said. "According to Node.js, this corruption can lead to a process crash, disclosure of sensitive process memory, or remote code execution. Exposure therefore depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled compressed data to the affected decoder." ELLIO also reported on Monday that its sensors "have recorded CVE-2026-111497 exploit traffic in the wild, carrying the public exploit that we confirmed gets a shell on vulnerable builds." The activity originates from "94.154.43[.]7," an IP address geolocated to the Netherlands that has also engaged in exploitation efforts targeting PHP2Shell, two critical flaws in PHP that could result in unauthenticated remote code execution. "The attacker's payload is a genuine, correctly-structured Node2Shell exploitation attempt for node v24.22.0 – the Brotli stream, staged displacement, pivot pair, and delivery are all correct and identical to the public tooling," ELLIO said. "This is indicative of the RCE being adopted by an operator focused on mass exploitation." The fact that Brotli is a widely distributed open-source library and adopted by numerous projects has provoked an emergency response, prompting various vendors to release patches or assess if their products are affected by the flaw. This includes PHP, which has shipped versions 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1, and 8.2.35-1, as well as Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, .NET, Python, ClickHouse, the PHP Brotli extension, and the Ruby "brotli" gem. Links to some of the advisories are below - Amazon Linux Bun Cisco Cloudflare CloudLinux Envoy Proxy F5 Fortinet Imperva Istio Microsoft Azure Microsoft .NET Node.js Palo Alto Networks PHP Qualys Red Hat Safe Security Strapi Tanium Tenable Ubuntu Upwind "Node.js fixed the vulnerability in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1," Akamai said. "The Node.js advisory does not offer a workaround, so upgrading is the only complete remediation. Organizations running a discontinued release line should move to a supported release line." Google-owned Wiz has warned that "91% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 and 82% of cloud environments have publicly exposed Node.js instances." "Node2Shell is not a bug in every Node.js service, but a bug in services that decode attacker-influenced Brotli," Sysdig said. "Express 5 with default JSON parsing puts a large number of instances of them in that group. The demonstrated impact thus far is crashes at scale and code execution in a narrow configuration, so patch order should follow reachability." Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 10, 2026, to apply the necessary fixes against the two flaws.

1rz157u.text: The GMO Group has urged customers to disconnect their systems from the internet and shut down computers after a threat actor who breached the company’s Onamae Desktop Cloud threatened to launch a ransomware attack today. The company later confirmed that data belonging to both the company and its customers had been published online. The alert concerns a cyberattack on Onamae Desktop Cloud, a popular VPS provider in Japan operated by GMO Internet, a member of GMO Internet Group and one of Japan's largest domain registrars. Last week, the company announced it detected an intrusion on October 20 that could have installed malware on up to 26,739 customers' servers. To minimize the risk, the company shut down the servers and reduced service availability before launching an investigation. The internet company assured customers that their payment information had not been exposed but warned that MetaTrader 4 and MetaTrader 5 (MT4/MT5) credentials and trading-account details may have been exposed or compromised. It urged customers to reset their passwords and terminate active sessions. Cyberattack escalation Subsequent updates from the company confirmed that data had been stolen and that the attacker was demanding a ransom of ¥8 billion ($50 million), which GMO said it would not pay. Instead, the company announced it would compensate each customer ¥5,000 ($30) for the inconvenience caused. On October 26, GMO warned that threat actors planned to leak customer information online and trigger a ransomware payload planted on customer servers earlier in the attack. The next day, the company asked customers to disconnect their PCs from the internet, shut them down, and unplug all cables before noon, while it worked with Trend Micro to recover from the cyberattack. “Once you have a backup, disconnect the network, power it down, and unplug the cord that connects to your PC,” advised GMO to customers. Instructions to customers Source: GMO The company said it was scanning customer systems to determine whether malware was still present, and offered equivalent PC replacements to those who suffered damages from a ransomware attack. In a report published earlier today, GMO confirmed that the threat actor had published company and customer data, prompting efforts to verify the authenticity of the leaked information. For customers whose information was exposed, GMO said it will consider additional financial compensation. It appears that the attacker never acted on their threat, as no ransomware was activated on customer machines. The company warned people and the media not to disseminate the exposed information, announcing it will take legal action against those who do, while reaffirming its refusal to pay the attackers. 1xvhmue.text: OpenAI confirmed GPT-6.1 Terra is safer overall than some of its older models, but its safety testing also found other problems. According to OpenAI, GPT-6.1 Terra showed higher rates of exfiltration, destructive actions, and attempts to bypass restrictions than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI performed simulations across approximately 48,690 matched tasks and found that Terra received 22 severity-3-or-higher flags, or 0.045%. For comparison, GPT-6 Sol received 38, while GPT-5.6 Sol received 61. "GPT-6.1 Terra received approximately 42% fewer severity level 3 or higher flags than GPT-6 Sol and 64% fewer than GPT-5.6 Sol," OpenAI noted in its system card. Cybersecurity Safety Training and Evaluation (Higher is better) However, that is no longer the case when you compare Terra with other newer models on less severe behaviors. "Relative to GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra, we observed higher rates of flags for concealing uncertainty, circumventing restrictions, exfiltration, other misalignment, destructive action and inbound prompt injection," OpenAI explained. Terra is clearly safer overall, but we can't overlook the other potential security issues it has, and this is true for all models shipping in the market, including Claude. Terra also performed more unauthorized actions in one test OpenAI also tested what happens when Terra needs to deal with messages from other AI agents while working through blocked coding tasks. Terra attempted to communicate with those apparent peers in 65% of tests and ultimately performed the specified unauthorized action in 13.75%, or 11 of 80 samples. OpenAI found that GPT-6.1 Sol did so in just 1.25%. "These results indicate that performance is comparable to 6.0 Sol," OpenAI noted, adding that much of the regression against GPT-6.1 Sol involved promises of future help that Terra indicated it would not actually carry out. OpenAI warns that these tests were conducted in simulated environments, so the results may not necessarily reflect how GPT-6.1 Terra behaves in real-world production environments. But we still aren't seeing meaningful improvements across every area of security, even as these companies claim their models can control computers and code better. 1c2fg1h.text: The University of New Mexico Health Sciences Center disclosed a cyberattack that caused system outages and disrupted patient care and academic activities. On Monday, UNM Health, the university’s healthcare provider, began temporarily limiting new patient admissions, diverting ambulances to nearby hospitals, and suspending outpatient surgeries and appointments. In an update on the incident, UNM said UNM Hospital and Sandoval Regional Medical Center remain open, and all clinics will resume scheduled appointments and procedures starting today, Tuesday, October 27. Regarding emergencies, the healthcare organization advised that people should call 911. However, today’s classes at its four health sciences schools are canceled, and nonessential HSC employees were instructed to stay home. UNM Health is a major statewide provider of specialist care with more than 1 million patient visits annually. Its flagship UNM Hospital in Albuquerque houses New Mexico’s only Level I trauma center, treating the most seriously injured patients. Byod ransomware claims the attack UNM did not disclose the type of cyberattack it suffered, but BleepingComputer found that a new ransomware group called Byod had claimed the attack. In a post on their data leak site, the threat actor said it had compromised 36,000 systems across UNM’s main campus and hospital environments, including Active Directory forests, Group Policy infrastructure, the entire Microsoft Entra tenant, and two Oracle databases. "This is your entire network and infrastructure compromised, the entire university COMPLETELY," the threat actor said. They claim access to student and employee personal data, including: Social Security numbers (SSNs) HR, payroll, and Banner student records Internal emails Research data Hospital appointment data Patient information Cerner EHR rosters In an attempt to force a payment, Byod ransomware said it would take down the breach post after the university initiated communication, likely for negotiating a ransom. BleepingComputer has reached out to UNM Health Sciences with a request for comment about these data theft allegations, but we have not received a response. In a new post today, Byod ransomware said it would provide free keys that decrypt locked systems at healthcare facilities. Caption Furthermore, the threat actor promised to pay up to $2,500 for every patient affected by the cyberattack. "We have morals and we have a heart, we are not villains, but we will still continue to hold companies responsible for bad security leading to the compromise of any customer data," the cybercriminals said. However, the threat actor also said that it would keep all the stolen data. Byod is a new ransomware gang that currently lists six victims on its data leak site. For three of them, it has already leaked the allegedly stolen data. On its FAQ page, the threat group claims it is doing “pentesting” to expose vulnerabilities and hold data controllers accountable for breaches. Source: BleepingComputer Byod says no target is off-limits, but it selects victims after an initial assessment identifies a target of interest. The group says it focuses on “those at the top who look at consumers and/or customers as a number or another dollar in their pockets.” The UNM Health Sciences said today that all its critical electronic systems are back online and all UNM Health hospitals are fully open. Ambulance traffic is now operating normally, and all clinics have resumed scheduled appointments and procedures. The university said the quick recovery was possible due to IT security teams working "with external partners to secure the network." "Their assessment determined that the event affected some end-user devices but did not penetrate core systems or servers," UNM Health Sciences Center notes. Patients who received care at UNM hospitals, as well as staff and students who work and study there, are advised to remain vigilant for unsolicited communications and phishing attacks. 1854l2s.text: A credit card skimming group reportedly compromised a shared analytics script used by e-commerce platform Convertr to steal shoppers’ payment data during checkout. The campaign was identified on October 24 and has been attributed to a Brazilian gang, active since at least July 2024, that focuses on infecting online stores running Magento, OpenCart, and WooCommerce platforms. Convertr is a Brazilian e-commerce platform that powers online stores and checkout systems for dozens of major fashion brands in the country, handling R$2 billion ($370M) in sales. E-commerce security firm Sansec says that the attacker modified the Plausible tracker file hosted on a self-managed server operated by Convertr. Ecommerce cybersecurity company Sansec says that the attacker modified the tracker file on a self-hosted server for Plausible, an open source alternative to Google Analytics, managed by Convertr. Sansec suspects the attackers exploited CVE-2026-8467, an unauthenticated command-execution vulnerability affecting Convertr’s outdated Plausible Community Edition installation, to gain initial access. However, this hasn’t been confirmed. After gaining access, the attackers injected malicious code into a legitimate Plausible analytics tracker hosted on Convertr’s infrastructure, which loads on the checkout pages of all merchants using the platform. The Magecart attack chain Source: Sansec Sansec says that earlier versions of the skimmer used generic payment-field patterns, but by October 26, the attackers pushed a more refined version that specifically targeted Convertr’s exact payment API field names. The injected skimmer was configured to steal the following data types from checkout pages: Payment card number Expiration date CVVs code Cardholder name CPF taxpayer identification number The researchers suggest that those who paid by card on a Brazilian store that contained the ‘checkout.convertr’ string in the checkout address page since October 24 should contact their bank immediately and ask to block their card. In an update today, Sansec confirmed that Convertr "removed the skimmer and upgraded Plausible to a patched version," noting that the company announced it was notifying affected merchants and payment providers. BleepingComputer has contacted Convertr for a statement on the incident, but we have not received a response yet. Sansec researchers warned that browser caching could keep the malicious script active on impacted sites for up to 24 hours after cleanup, so customers should clear their cache before placing new orders, even after the threat has been eliminated. One way to protect payment card details when shopping online is to use disposable virtual cards that expire immediately after a transaction. 1ky4mnl.text: A former ransomware hacker was sentenced to 70 months in prison after pleading guilty last year to charges tied to several cyberattacks on hospitals, government entities and more. Artem Stryzhak, a 36-year-old from Ukraine, was an affiliate of the Nefilim ransomware group while living in Barcelona, Spain. Throughout 2021, Stryzhak used Nefilim to launch attacks on organizations in the U.S., Canada and Australia. Stryzhak paid Nefilim administrators, including indicted co-conspirator Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, a 20% fee of all ransoms extorted from victims. Stryzhak eventually moved on from Nefilim and joined the Hive ransomware gang — working with the group from October 2021 to January 2023. Tymoshchuk has evaded capture. Stryzhak helped Hive attack organizations throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, targeting hospitals, governments and businesses. The group encrypted thousands of victims across 80 countries and earned millions in ransom payments throughout its run as a prominent ransomware gang. “Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals,” said Assistant FBI Director Brett Leatherman. “These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses.” Prosecutors listed one incident where a hospital was unable to accept new patients during the pandemic due to a Hive ransomware attack. The Hive ransomware gang was disrupted by the FBI after a months-long operation. Stryzhak was eventually arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited last April. He pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud, extortion, and related activity in connection with computers. “This sentence concludes a years-long, multi-continent investigation into a defendant who participated in cyberattacks against Americans’ businesses and health care,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva. Prosecutors said they are still searching for Tymoshchuk, who is also accused of being an administrator for the LockerGoga and MegaCortex ransomware gangs. U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said they “remain determined to capture Volodymyr Tymoshchuk.” The DOJ previously issued an $11 million reward for information on Tymoshchuk’s whereabouts and a $15 million reward for information on other members of Hive. No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

1ie746l.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of three cyber attacks targeting organizations in Japan in which artificial intelligence (AI) was a key element, either in the driving seat or to assist a human operator. TrendAI, which analyzed three exposed server environments used by threat actors to conduct the malicious cyber operations, described them as distinct from previously published attacks that have leveraged ARTEX, an autonomous AI penetration testing framework, to single out entities in South Korea and Japan. "These environments held reconnaissance and attack tools, scripts, target lists, results, logs, and command histories," security researchers Bakuei Matsukawa and Joseph C Chen said. "They ranged from workspaces used largely by hand by skilled operators to AI-agent platforms that automated the entire workflow, including command and control." The first of the three attacks has been found to abuse CyberStrikeAI, another open-source penetration testing tool that was previously put to use in an attack campaign targeting Fortinet FortiGate appliances. The activity was concentrated in a short period in October 2026. The AI-driven activity leverages the offensive security tool to automate various aspects of the attack lifecycle into a repeatable workflow, beginning with reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery and validation, and exploitation, to command-and-control (C2), persistence, data exfiltration, and automated reporting. This involves delegating the work among 44 agents to handle various aspects of the attack, while also enabling the generation of forms and fake login pages in the Japanese language. "In a short period, at least 19 identifiable organizations, including at least 16 in Japan, were subjected to validation activity," Trend Micro's enterprise security division said. "Each had a report in the same format and an index of evidence. These were outputs of a structured process run by the platform, rather than ad hoc notes left by an operator." The second case has been characterized as a human-led attack with assistance from a large language model (LLM) to accelerate planning and tool development. Analysis of the infrastructure and artifacts indicates that the campaign is also designed to target AI workflow platforms and inference services with an aim to obtain large amounts of inference capacity at low cost. One of the intrusions is said to have targeted a geographic information system (GIS) server exposed with default credentials, resulting in the theft of cadastral and commercial records, Windows credentials, and email data. The entire campaign lasted for 24 days in August and September 2026. The third instance is where the AI's role has been found to be confined to developing the operator's tools and scripts, suggesting a limited role played by the technology in a series of campaigns designed to target edge devices from Cisco, Citrix, F5, and Yamaha using published vulnerabilities, management functions, or credentials present in configuration files. The threat actor is estimated to have run at least six campaigns from January to October 2026, opportunistically striking exposed VPN devices and WebLogic servers. "The operator was experienced, with established practices for automation and evidence management," the researchers said. There is currently no evidence at this stage that suggests these three incidents share an operator. It's also unknown if the attacks have targeted other regions and what AI models are being used to pull off the attacks. That said, the attacks involving these threat actors are not restricted to Japan and neighboring countries like South Korea. The operator behind the first case has targeted organizations in Taiwan and Hong Kong, while the third case featured organizations in the U.K., France, Italy, Qatar, and Colombia in its WebLogic discovery lists. "AI has increased the attackers' workforce, but the work still consists of looking for unlocked doors," TrendAI said. "The types of doors and the weaknesses that leave them open have not changed. What has changed is the ability to try thousands at once, adapt to the target country's language, and continue without fatigue." The development coincides with the discovery of multiple campaigns in which threat actors of varied motivations have integrated agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows, allowing them to speed up research, malware development, social engineering, and other parts of an attack. To make matters worse, AI is being increasingly used to accelerate reconnaissance, automate decision-making, and industrialize social engineering, shortening the time between exposure and exploitation of security flaws. According to Microsoft's 2026 Digital Defense Report, AI has collapsed the median time from vulnerability discovery to weaponization to well below 24 hours. The adoption of AI by bad actors is reducing the time, expertise, and cost required to discover and exploit weaknesses, at the same allowing attackers and defenders alike to operate with greater speed, scale, and autonomy, the Windows maker added. "The key issue is not simply whether an actor has frontier AI," Trend Micro said. "Access to capable models can already produce meaningful operational gains. Ecosystem depth, however, determines how reliably, independently, and at what scale those capabilities can be sustained." "AI is no longer an experimental capability for APT groups; it is an operational component embedded directly into campaigns." The growing demand for AI tools by threat actors has also opened up a new monetization avenue that peddles stolen AI provider session tokens and offensive AI tools APEX AI, MessiahGPT, and DarkGPT, further commoditizing cybercrime and lowering the barrier to entry for carrying out advanced, persistent, and evasive attacks. Last week, Microsoft revealed that a China-state-aligned threat actor compromised a ConnectWise cloud backup application and used ARTEX to sign in to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. The activity has been attributed to Storm-0940, which it said has used the framework since as early as September 2026 to automate password-spraying attacks on hundreds of organizations. "While the majority of the targeting wasn't successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time," Microsoft said. "Storm-0940's activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations." According to local media reports from South Korea, authorities have identified seven suspects linked to a cybercrime operation that broke into more than 90 organizations in the country, most of which involved ARTEX. The 32-year-old mastermind behind the activity is alleged to have worked at a cybersecurity company between 2019 and 2022, gaining expertise in penetration testing. In 38 of the incidents, the threat actors demanded ransom payments of 360 million won ($270,000) in exchange for not leaking the stolen data. More than 8.2 million records are believed to have been siphoned from compromised organizations. Some of the other AI-oriented campaigns that have been documented in recent weeks are listed below - A financially-motivated threat actor operating under the handle BUGSTER configured the Hermes Agent framework with DeepSeek V4 as its reasoning engine and Cursor as a secondary tool (both with safety controls disabled) to run a WordPress brute-force campaign against an Indian university's website and generate a REST API enumeration report. The attacker also breached a second Indian public university, exfiltrating a database of more than 5,200 records, including personally identifiable information (PII) on students. A third attack enumerated an Indian site on a popular e-commerce platform to extract a storefront API token, admin email addresses, phone numbers, and payment merchant IDs. "The actor also built specialized AI bot profiles to acquire VoIP fraud expertise through conversation and maintained automated pipelines for Wi-Fi password cracking and cryptocurrency whale reconnaissance (i.e., identifying large cryptocurrency holders)," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Notably, the Wi-Fi cracking capability requires close physical proximity to the target, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations." An e-crime group named CyberCartel has been observed using a multi-agent system called CARLIY0S to coordinate attacks against banks and payment providers across Latin America. The framework employs a cognitive swarm comprising four role-specialized Claude models that "debate each target and defer to one arbiter" before the main orchestrator acts. "The group assigned different roles to commercial AI models to analyze targets, develop attacks, and coordinate operations," Straiker said. Threat actors have developed an offensive AI agent designed to hijack exposed AI endpoints to run autonomous attacks, with instructions allowing it to carry out up to 100,000 steps without human approval while the legitimate owner of the exposed endpoint pays for the inference. The system features a malicious loop called Skynet mode that employs a set of 74 tools to scan for targets, infect them, deploy cryptocurrency miners, and reinfect compromised hosts. An affiliate for the The Gentlemen ransomware operation has used Anthropic Claude Code during intrusions into at least six organizations in late June 2026, including to generate and execute reconnaissance and exploitation commands, write malicious scripts, modify firewall policies, and identify high-value business systems. A credential-harvesting operation codenamed Zerofot built a scanner named "auto_scan" that integrated OpenAI Codex and Claude Code to harvest thousands of API keys and tokens from thousands of exposed hosts across the internet. An AI-generated Python framework called RAGE has been used to scan internet-facing services (e.g., Redis, Elasticsearch, Docker, Apache Tomcat, Jenkins, Hadoop YARN, Confluence, and Supervisord), exploit vulnerable deployments, capture credentials, and deploy cryptocurrency miners. A human operator employed frontier AI models to breach an enterprise network autonomously over a 10-hour period. "The actor breached a publicly accessible web service to tunnel into the network, deploying an automated recon agent to map internal microservices," Unit 42 said. "Sub-agents combed enterprise code repositories, extracting hard-coded tokens and service passwords." The attacker then harvested master administrative credentials and hijacked an enterprise code application to exfiltrate cloud access keys. The stolen cloud keys were then used to turn the victim's AI endpoints into post-compromise infrastructure. A suspected Russian-speaking cyber actor used an AI-assisted workflow to exploit PaperCut NG/MF servers and compromise hundreds of instances. "The campaign extended beyond initial exploitation into a structured post-exploitation pipeline covering Windows credential collection, service-credential harvesting, internal network pivoting, Metasploit automation, and victim packaging," Hunt.io said. A Chinese-speaking threat actor has breached websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins, using an autonomous penetration testing engine called Cairn, tasking it to probe targets, search for security weaknesses that could lead to code execution or account takeover, attempt to break in, and steal sensitive data. "AI is serving as a force multiplier and an expanding attack surface at the same time," Rapid7 said. "Generative AI is accelerating established attack methods by reducing the time, skill, and coordination previously required to execute them at scale." "Rather than introducing entirely new categories of exploitation, threat actors are integrating AI into existing workflows to industrialize phishing, automate reconnaissance, and refine malicious scripts with greater speed and precision."

egk4lk.text: Microsoft has released out-of-band (OOB) Windows updates to remove trust in certificates tied to compromised eMudhra certificate authority keys, protecting systems that do not receive automatic certificate trust updates. The KB5134133 update for Windows 11 versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 and the KB5134125 update for Windows 10 versions 21H2 and 22H2 were released on October 26. The updates are for systems without Internet access, devices that cannot access Microsoft's certificate-update service, and those where automatic Certificate Trust List (CTL) updates have been disabled. The updates were released after the discovery of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority private keys that were so weak they could be recovered almost instantly. All eight keys were generated in April 2025 and had values smaller than 256, allowing anyone to recover them by testing just 256 possible numbers. The compromised keys could have allowed attackers to forge certificates for legitimate websites and intercept encrypted communications. After the disclosure, eMudhra revoked the eight compromised intermediate certificates, and Mozilla, Google, Apple, and other software vendors also began revoking them. In response, Microsoft previously updated the Windows Disallowed Certificate Trust List to block the eight affected intermediate certificate authorities, including six used for TLS and two for code signing. The company also released a CRLSet update for Microsoft Edge and WebView2 to block affected TLS certificates, which enabled the block without requiring a browser update. Microsoft is now taking further steps by removing seven certificates associated with the affected certificate hierarchies from its Windows trust list. "On October 26, Microsoft released an out-of-band Windows update that removes seven certificates associated with the affected hierarchies: six eMudhra G3 roots and an AAA Certificate Services cross-sign, from the Windows trust list," Microsoft explained. The new update goes further by also removing trust in the eMudhra root certificates used to verify other certificates issued by the CA. Microsoft says the same seven certificates will also be removed from the Edge trust list on October 27. "Removing a root from a trust list is not the same as revoking the known impacted intermediate certificate authorities," explains Microsoft. "This is a separate trust decision, broader than blocking the identified compromised intermediate keys. Organizations with a specific compatibility need may choose to trust a certificate locally, subject to their own security assessment and policies." The company advises admins to install the update on disconnected Windows systems and identify any certificates that depend on the removed roots, as they may need to be replaced. Microsoft is also investigating the remaining eMudhra roots and may make additional trust changes as needed. td6wea.text: Agent decision logs and telemetry data belonging to Warp agentic development environment users were exposed in an attack on a third-party vendor in the project’s infrastructure. The company’s founder and CEO, Zach Lloyd, estimates that "roughly 1% of Warp users may have been impacted," but external experts are helping with the ongoing investigation. Warp is a popular developer tool that started as a modern terminal and evolved into an agentic development environment (ADE) that allows developers to direct AI agents to write and test code and deploy software. The environment provides a terminal, a code editor, task orchestration, and agent review tools in a single workspace. The project's website says the platform has at least 800,000 users. “On Friday, we became aware of what we believe to be an active and narrow-banded exploitation of a vendor in Warp's infrastructure,” Lloyd stated. “We detected the operation within hours and were able to remediate and mitigate the impact,” the CEO added. Although agent traces and telemetry were identified as potentially affected data, the company did not clarify whether the exposed information included source code, prompts, credentials, or other sensitive details. Analysis of the incident suggests that the attack was powered by "an agent swarm" that relied on "a very sophisticated penetration and escalation technique." Lloyd said that Warp has contacted the third-party vendor about the vulnerability, but no details have been shared. The platform has notified users identified to be impacted. The cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has also been engaged to assist with the investigation, while the platform has also informed law enforcement authorities. The incident at Warp follows an incident at AI coding platform OpenCode, which notified users last week that a security breach exposed stored API keys used with external providers. The incident affected a small percentage of OpenCode users, about 1.4%, and led to unauthorized charges of up to $1,700 for some. 1wld6m5.text: The Tailscale security team is working to patch almost a dozen security vulnerabilities that could be exploited to steal credentials, crash servers, gain root privileges, and more. Tailscale develops a software-defined mesh virtual private network (VPN) built on WireGuard that lets users connect computers, servers, and cloud instances from anywhere to the same encrypted mesh network ("tailnet") via direct peer-to-peer (P2P) connections. Cyberdione Labs discovered 11 flaws (collectively known as Tailworm) that still lack patches during a security audit of Tailscale 1.104.2 and the self-hosted headscale v0.29.5 control server. "All findings were verified by reproduction in a lab environment on unmodified, released software (tailscale v1.104.2, headscale v0.29.5)," said Erica Windisch, founder of Cyberdione Labs, who reported the flaws to Tailscale and publicly released the details. "It is the opinion of the researchers that rapid awareness of these flaws will expediate remediation across impacted devices. These vulnerabilities were not introduced by the researchers, but were discovered, and discovered with low effort." The table below classifies the security issues by the component they affect. The most critical issue is in Tailscale's SSH server and could let authorized attackers gain code execution with root privileges through Unix-socket forwarding on a targeted tailnet. Component / feature Mechanism (what breaks) Attacker requirement Principal outcome Tailscale SSH (tailscaled's embedded SSH server, running as root) Unix-socket forwarding (ssh -R/-L) performs path checks and file operations as root; races and missing privilege drop let an ordinary session replace, dial, or delete privileged resources One approved device + one SSH policy rule (forwarding granted automatically on headscale; per-rule on SaaS) Root execution on target servers; capture of enrollment keys; arbitrary root-file deletion Tailscale app connectors (conn25, experimental) Connector translates traffic to attacker-chosen destinations with no validation; network ACLs are never consulted for the true destination A device granted the connector capability Reach cloud metadata (credential theft), internal LANs, and — in Kubernetes — every cluster service headscale control server (self-hosted deployments) Unauthenticated resource exhaustion (memory growth, cache eviction) Internet reachability; no account Control-server crash loop; blocking of new-device onboarding org-wide Tailscale DERP client (relay connection in every agent) Unbounded read of a malicious relay's response Ability to position/point a client at a hostile relay Client-agent memory exhaustion tailscale serve (local service exposure) TCP-forward to a unix socket lacks a guard present on the HTTP path; plus a race in per-mount authorization Operator configures the forward (or a peer races the mount check) Remote administrative-API access to the node; minority of requests bypass app authz On Monday, the Tailscale team said it received Cyberdione Labs' report and was working on patches to address these security issues by the end of today. The developers also confirmed that the reported flaws are "serious" as they could let threat actors with permissions on targeted systems take actions with escalated privileges. "Most of the Tailscale SSH issues we've identified concern privilege escalation. In some circumstances, someone already authorized to connect over Tailscale SSH may be able to perform actions beyond the permissions of their configured local user, including potentially gaining elevated privileges," Tailscale said. "These are serious security issues, and we're treating them accordingly. Exploitation depends on the permissions granted to the connecting user or device, the system's configuration, and other conditions. We're continuing to verify the full scope of the findings and which configurations may be affected." However, despite the severity of the issues, Tailscale said it doesn't recommend that users disable the Tailscale SSH feature. "If you want to jump to the most important part, based on our current assessment, we're not recommending that everyone disable Tailscale SSH," said Mike Shaver, VP of Engineering at Tailscale. Instead, the Tailscale team shared measures that should mitigate some of these flaws: Review SSH access policies. Limit access to the users and devices that need it. Disable SSH forwarding if you don't need it. Set TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1 in the tailscaled service environment and restart the service. This disables SSH forwarding without disabling Tailscale SSH entirely, and mitigates several of the more serious findings. Review access to sensitive systems. Consider temporarily tightening your Tailscale SSH access policies while we investigate, so that only the specific users and devices that need access can connect. The Tailscale devs aim to push a new version that fixes these issues by the end of Tuesday, October 27, and urged users to prepare to update and "apply the patched Tailscale client release when it becomes available."
