tygo3w.text: The GoAhead embedded web server loaded a certificate revocation list into its default TLS backend but never turned revocation checking on, so a revoked client certificate could still pass login on affected setups. The flaw is in builds that use the OpenSSL backend with mutual-TLS, where the server checks a client certificate and vice versa, and a revocation list is configured to block revoked certificates. That is a setup an operator turns on deliberately; a default build does not. GoAhead 6.1.1, released to device makers on August 2, 2026, and publicly published on October 12, fixes it. GoAhead is a small web server that device makers build into firmware to run management pages on routers, printers, gateways and industrial controllers. Its maker, EmbedThis, says it runs in hundreds of millions of devices. The flaw was found by Sébastien Féry of FoxIO, who described it and two other TLS problems in a write-up on October 26. On an affected build, the server loads the revocation list file at startup and reports no error, so an operator who configured it has every reason to think revocation is working. It is not. A client whose certificate was revoked, for example a stolen or retired device, completes the handshake as if the certificate were still valid and gets whatever access that identity allows. In FoxIO's test against GoAhead 6.1.0 with OpenSSL 3.6.2, a revoked certificate was accepted with issuer checking switched on. The OpenSSL advisory describes revoked client certificates as silently accepted. To be exploited, the build must use the OpenSSL backend with client certificates required, a trusted certificate authority bundle and issuer checking enabled, and a revocation list configured; the attacker must hold a certificate signed by a trusted authority and listed as revoked. Builds that use the Mbed TLS backend are unaffected; that backend checks revocation via a separate code path. The identifier on the advisory is CVE-2026-115881, rated 9.1 by EmbedThis. As of October 27, that identifier and the others below were not yet live in the public CVE and NVD databases; EmbedThis says it has requested them. The severity ratings are the vendor's own. Researchers cover two further problems, each tied to a specific TLS build. The versions and fixes differ, so the table below maps each by backend. TLS build What goes wrong Affected versions Fix or interim option OpenSSL (default) Revocation list loaded but never enforced; revoked client certificates accepted. CVE-2026-115881, rated 9.1. 3.4.5 through 6.1.0 Upgrade to 6.1.1. No interim option in the advisory. LibreSSL legacy verifier (3.2.x, 3.3.2–3.3.6) A client certificate chain longer than the limit is accepted when client certificates are required but issuer checking is off. CVE-2026-115884, rated 7.4. 6.1.0 and earlier on those LibreSSL versions Upgrade to 6.1.1, or turn issuer checking on with a trusted CA bundle, or use OpenSSL or LibreSSL 4.x. Mbed TLS A length typo sends a 1-byte Diffie-Hellman value instead of the full 2048-bit one, so a passive observer can decrypt the session. Rated 5.9. No CVE assigned. 4.0.2 through 6.1.0 Upgrade to 6.1.1, turn off finite-field DHE suites, or use the OpenSSL backend. The Mbed TLS problem only reaches a session if the client accepts the broken setup. OpenSSL, current Go, current Java, and mainstream browsers refuse a value that small and fall back to a stronger key exchange, so the session never completes. Clients without a minimum-size check, such as some embedded or custom ones, accept it, and then anyone who recorded the traffic can work out the key and read the session. TLS 1.3 and ECDHE sessions are unaffected, and Mbed TLS 4.x removed the key exchange they rely on. The LibreSSL problem allows an attacker to present a certificate chain longer than GoAhead's 10-certificate limit and still complete the handshake as an authenticated client, without any trusted key. It appears only on builds linked against the older LibreSSL versions listed above and only where client certificates are required with issuer checking off. OpenSSL, BoringSSL, AWS-LC and LibreSSL 4.x reject the over-long chain. Which backend and settings a build uses are chosen when the firmware is compiled, so a device owner cannot tell from the outside which apply. That is also why the fix is slow to arrive: GoAhead 6.1.1 is a drop-in replacement that device makers rebuild and ship as a firmware update, and an owner gets it only when their manufacturer does so. Whether any manufacturer has shipped it is not known. As of October 27, no source reported any of these problems being used in attacks. EmbedThis's policy is to end a disclosure embargo and publish early if a flaw is being exploited or disclosed by someone else, so the coordinated October 12 release is consistent with no known attacks. However, it does not prove there are none. EmbedThis notifies customers of security updates through its Builder portal. FoxIO has published proof-of-concept code and offers fingerprints through its JA4Scan tool to find GoAhead servers by backend. The tool is free, but its source is available only on request, and a fingerprint identifies a build, not a confirmed-vulnerable server. None of the device makers EmbedThis lists as GoAhead users, which include HP, Oracle, Siemens, Canon, Rockwell, D-Link and Comcast, has been shown to run an affected backend and setting. The affected population is not established. The same 6.1.1 release closes 11 advisories in all, three of them rated critical. One is a login bypass: on a build using HTTP Basic or form login, an attacker who knows a valid username can sign in with any password if that user's stored password is in the newer Blowfish format, which GoAhead added in version 6.1.0. EmbedThis says form login is the default for its built-in administration pages. After upgrading, EmbedThis recommends ending active sessions, restarting the server, and changing Blowfish-stored passwords.

vuas5r.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 27, 2026Vulnerability / Mobile Security Apple on Monday backported fixes for a high-severity security flaw that was exploited in real-world cyber attacks to older devices. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-86950 (CVSS score: 8.8), is an out-of-bounds write affecting CoreGraphics that could result in arbitrary code execution when processing a maliciously crafted file. Patches for the flaw were released last month by Apple in versions iOS 26.7.1, iPadOS 26.7.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1, acknowledging that it may have been exploited in sophisticated attacks against specific individuals using devices running iOS before iOS 27. The fixes have now been expanded to include iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11, which support iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, iPad 7th generation, iPad Air 4th generation and later, iPad 9th generation and later, and iPad mini 6th generation and later. "Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27," the company said. iOS 18.7.11 and iPadOS 18.7.11 also address a logic issue in Audio (CVE-2026-65339) that could be exploited by an app to leak sensitive user information and an access vulnerability in CoreMedia (CVE-2026-86990) that could be abused by a malicious app to access the camera without user permission. The release comes as Apple shipped iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS Golden Gate 27.2, tvOS 27.2, watchOS 27.2, visionOS 27.2, and Safari 27.2, fixing hundreds of vulnerabilities, including many in AppleAVD, CoreAudio, ImageIO, kernel, Model I/O, Screen Sharing Server, Spotlight, StorageKit, and WebKit. Notable among the defects is an authorization issue in Apple Intelligence (CVE-2026-86987) that could be exploited by a remote attacker to access sensitive user data. The iPhone maker said the issue was addressed in iOS and iPadOS with improved entitlement checks. Although Apple makes no mention of any of these flaws being exploited in the wild, it's always a good practice to update the devices to the latest version for optimal protection.

iuqei3.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 27, 2026Vulnerability / Mobile Security Microsoft has fixed a flaw in its Authenticator app for Android that let a malicious app with no permissions pose as a trusted Microsoft app, such as Teams, and collect sign-in tokens for a victim's work account. Microsoft tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-80097 and fixed it in Authenticator for Android version 6.2606.4246, so anyone using the app should update. In the researchers' tests, the tokens gave full access to the account's email, files, and calendar. Microsoft says exploitation also needs the victim to complete a sign-in step in Authenticator, and that the flaw has not been used in attacks. The research comes from Ofek Levin, working through a fellowship program at the security firm Enclave, which published the technical details on October 23, 2026. Microsoft assigned the CVE on September 8 and rated it 8.6 on the CVSS scale, which it labels "Important." On Android, Authenticator does more than show six-digit codes. It also acts as a broker: when Teams, Outlook, or another Microsoft app needs to sign a user in, it asks Authenticator, and Authenticator hands back a token, a digital pass that proves the user is logged in. Because the broker controls access to the entire account, it should be careful about which app it grants a token to. The flaw let the wrong app get one. Authenticator exposes a component, an activity named AccountChooserActivity, that any app on the device can start. When the attacker's app started it, Authenticator built its token request from values the attacker's app supplied, including the name of the app it claimed to be. The app said it was Teams, and the broker believed it. A signature check was supposed to stop this, but it did not. The check looked up the real signature of the app being impersonated and confirmed the request matched it. Because Teams was genuinely installed on the device, its real signature was there to read, so the check passed. Authenticator could also see which app had actually made the request, Enclave found, but it did not use that to decide whether to hand over a token. In Enclave's tests, posing as Teams and requesting Microsoft Graph tokens returned permissions to read and send mail, read and write files, and read and write calendars, among others. Microsoft describes the result more generally: a successful attacker could authenticate as the signed-in user and reach that user's resources. The tokens apply to the work account signed into Authenticator on that device, not to other accounts. The two accounts disagree on one point a reader should weigh. Enclave reported that its proof of concept returned tokens without any user interaction, other than the presence of a signed-in account. Microsoft's advisory says exploitation requires installing a malicious app on the device and convincing the user to complete an authentication flow in Authenticator. Its CVSS score also indicates that the flaw requires user interaction. Microsoft says the flaw has not been exploited and was not publicly disclosed before the fix, and rates exploitation as "less likely." It was part of the company's September 2026 Patch Tuesday and was not one of the two Windows flaws flagged that month as already under attack. The vulnerability is not listed in the U.S. CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of October 26, 2026. The fix is to update Microsoft Authenticator for Android to version 6.2606.4246 or later, as linked in Microsoft's advisory. Organizations that manage Android devices can require that minimum version through their device management. Microsoft's advisory gives the fix but does not say whether updating cancels any token a malicious app may already have obtained, so that remains unclear from the available sources.

y4sb66.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 27, 2026Cryptocurrency / Data Breach An attacker who gained access to Keystone's website obtained the key that its hardware wallets use to prove they are genuine, the company said in a statement on October 26. Someone with that key could build counterfeit devices that pass the online check owners use to verify a Keystone. A buyer who trusted a counterfeit could have their crypto stolen, but the incident did not involve owners' recovery phrases or wallet private keys. Keystone will destroy 18,835 unsold devices that carry the key, and all new devices will get a new one. Keystone found the unauthorized access on October 20, and its advice to owners depends on when a device arrived. For a device received after that date with the old key, the company said: "Even if such a device passes authentication, we cannot completely rule out the possibility that it is counterfeit." Owners of such a device should contact Keystone support and use it only after the company confirms it is genuine. A device delivered before October 20 that passes the check can be considered genuine and used normally, according to Keystone. The company has not said when the attacker first got in. The attacker exploited a vulnerability in a third-party data monitoring tool used by Keystone's website to escalate privileges, according to the company. That let the attacker obtain customer data and the key. Keystone blocked the attacker's access on October 20 and has since fixed the vulnerability. It has not said where the key was stored. How the Device Check Works The owner scans a QR code on Keystone's verification page with the device, then enters the code the device displays on the page. In Keystone's open-source firmware, the QR code carries that code in encrypted form, and the device decrypts it with its stored key. So a correct code shows that the device holds the key. The key is used only for this check. It plays no part in creating recovery phrases, deriving private keys, or signing transactions. Anyone with a copy of the key could produce the right codes, so a counterfeit device carrying it could pass the check. Such devices could be sold or shipped to customers, leading to the theft of their crypto, Keystone said. The company has not reported any counterfeit devices or thefts. The key is written into each device during manufacturing and cannot be erased or rewritten. The firmware keeps it in memory, which can be written only once, and refuses to accept a second key. So devices already made cannot be switched to the new key. Customer Records Keystone first disclosed the breach on October 24, saying a third party had obtained customers' shipping information. The incident affected 25,964 buyer records from purchases on Keystone's website between 2024 and 2026, the company said on October 26. The records hold names, contact details, shipping addresses, and order details. Keystone's online store runs on Shopify, which stored and managed the records. Payment card and bank details and government ID numbers were not involved, Keystone said. Purchase records from Amazon and Keystone's other sales channels were not affected. Keystone has also included 12,873 unpaid checkout records in its response as a precaution. These hold names, contact details, and shipping information from purchases that were never completed. Some of the affected data should already have been deleted. Keystone had promised to delete shipping information 180 days after each order. An automated tool Keystone built to erase records in bulk did not work reliably. Some deletions failed, and Keystone did not catch the failures in time. Keystone is shortening the period it retains customers' personal data from 180 days to 90 days, effective immediately. It has asked Shopify to delete buyers' personal data older than 90 days and expects that to be done on November 3. As of October 27, its privacy policy still listed 180 days. Keystone is emailing affected customers and plans a page where people can check whether their information was affected. What Keystone Owners Should Do Keystone's guidance covers these situations: Delivered before October 20: A device that passes the check can be used normally. Received after October 20 with the old key: Do not use the device until Keystone support, at support@keyst.one, confirms it is genuine. Keystone told these owners to follow instructions on its device verification page, but the page showed no such instructions as of October 27. Keystone has not said how to tell which key a device carries, or what owners who have already sent crypto to such a device should do. Waiting on an order from Keystone's website: Shipping is paused until devices with the new key are ready. As of October 27, the store listed the Keystone 3 Pro as a pre-order expected to ship within 4 to 6 weeks. Bought through Amazon or a reseller: The same guidance applies, because it is based on when a device arrived, not where it was bought. Keystone sells through Amazon official stores and authorized resellers. Keystone has not said whether devices with the old key are still on sale there. Already holding crypto with a Keystone: Owners do not need to move their crypto just because of the incident, Keystone said. Those with a device received after October 20 with the old key should still follow the steps above. Scam messages: Treat any call, text, email, or letter offering a refund, a replacement device, a recall, wallet verification, or help moving crypto as a scam. Keystone will not ask anyone to return a device. Never enter a recovery phrase into a device you did not order, and type keyst.one into your browser instead of following links.

1x0962e.text: The Hacker NewsOct 27, 2026Identity Security / Artificial Intelligence Fake login pages are nothing new, but generative AI is making them easier to build and more convincing. Attackers can recreate familiar login screens, impersonate trusted brands and tailor phishing attempts to specific employees or organizations. Some fake login pages go beyond stealing passwords. They can also capture MFA codes or hijack authenticated sessions, allowing attackers to gain access to corporate accounts even when additional security measures are in place. How AI is making fake login pages more convincing Attackers have long used fake login pages to steal credentials, but generative AI makes it easier to create convincing replicas of legitimate authentication portals. From company logos and page layouts to login prompts, these fraudulent pages can closely resemble the websites employees regularly access. AI also makes it easier to tailor phishing campaigns to specific organizations or employees. For example, attackers can create personalized IT notifications that direct employees to a fraudulent login page using the company's branding and familiar authentication prompts. These attacks often rely on lookalike domains that closely resemble legitimate web addresses, with subtle spelling changes or additional characters. Combined with realistic login pages and targeted messaging, these tactics make phishing attempts harder to recognize. While these techniques aren't new, generative AI lets attackers create, customize and adapt phishing campaigns more quickly and at a larger scale. The 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report found that phishing accounted for 44% of the AI-assisted initial-access techniques examined. How fake login pages lead to account takeovers Fake login pages can capture more than usernames and passwords. Some replicate multi-step authentication processes to collect MFA codes, which attackers can attempt to use before they expire to gain unauthorized access to corporate accounts and applications. More sophisticated attacks use Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) techniques to intercept authentication sessions. In these attacks, a fraudulent website acts as a proxy between the user and the legitimate service, relaying authentication requests in real time. After the user successfully authenticates, the attacker may capture a session cookie or authentication token and use it to access the account without completing another MFA challenge. This makes session hijacking particularly dangerous. Even with MFA enabled, attackers can potentially access accounts by stealing active session tokens. This lets them hijack an authenticated session without entering a password or completing another MFA challenge. Why traditional phishing defenses aren't always enough Security awareness training helps employees recognize phishing attempts, but convincing login page replicas can be difficult to distinguish from legitimate websites. Even experienced users can overlook subtle warning signs, particularly when a fraudulent page uses familiar branding and authentication prompts. Email filters, URL blocklists and website reputation services can stop many known phishing threats, but newly registered domains and short-lived phishing sites may evade detection. Attackers also distribute malicious links through text messages, collaboration platforms and search ads, letting phishing attempts bypass email-based defenses. URL inspection provides another layer of protection, but lookalike domains can be difficult to identify. A valid HTTPS connection also doesn't guarantee that a website is legitimate. These gaps highlight the need for security controls that can evaluate suspicious websites and detect potential credential-harvesting attempts before users enter their login information. How organizations can protect against credential theft Organizations can reduce the risk of credential theft by strengthening authentication, detecting suspicious login pages and limiting what attackers can access if an account is compromised. Use phishing-resistant MFA and passkeys: FIDO2 security keys and passkeys use cryptographic authentication tied to legitimate website domains, reducing the risk of credential theft through fraudulent login pages. Implement browser-level phishing protection: Browser-based security tools can detect look-alike domains, brand impersonation and suspicious URL patterns. AI-powered detection can help identify credential-harvesting sites and warn users before they enter sensitive information. Monitor authentication and session activity: Unusual sign-in locations, unfamiliar devices and suspicious session behavior can indicate account compromise. Continuous monitoring helps security teams identify and respond to potential account takeovers. Limit privileged access: Enforcing least-privilege policies and removing unnecessary standing privileges limits what attackers can access through compromised accounts. Just-in-time access further reduces the window of opportunity for abusing elevated permissions. Establish phishing response procedures: Organizations should have clear processes for reporting suspected phishing attempts, revoking compromised sessions, resetting credentials and investigating unauthorized access. Protecting credentials before they're exposed Phishing protection needs to extend beyond email filters and traditional detection methods to the point where users enter their credentials. Keeper's AI-powered Phishing Protection uses on-device AI to identify suspicious websites, including look-alike domains and spoofed login pages, warning users before they enter their credentials. By identifying suspicious websites earlier, organizations can reduce opportunities for credential harvesting and prevent stolen credentials from leading to account takeovers. Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Aranza Trevino at Keeper Security.

12obxc8.text: The North Korea-linked Lazarus Group has been attributed to a cyber espionage campaign dubbed Operation FlashHole targeting at least three organizations in South Korea spanning the construction, software, and wire-communication equipment manufacturing sectors. According to Russian cybersecurity company Kaspersky, the campaign has been active since at least July 2025. It's assessed to pick up from where Operation SyncHole left off. "The group targeted victims more selectively, sending spear‑phishing emails with links to fabricated but relevant sites, such as portfolio and résumé pages tailored to each target," Sojun Ryu, senior security researcher at Kaspersky GReAT, said in an exhaustive analysis. Operation SyncHole was first documented by Kaspersky in April 2025, detailing the state-sponsored adversary's targeting of South Korea's software, IT, financial, semiconductor manufacturing, and telecommunications industries since November 2024 to deliver malware such as ThreatNeedle, AGAMEMNON, wAgent, SIGNBT, and COPPERHEDGE. The attacks were characterized by the exploitation of a security flaw in iniLINE Cross EX for malware delivery. Cross EX is a mandatory financial security software program installed by South Korean internet users on their computers to support security software across various browser environments when accessing online banking and government services. The exploit was designed to launch the legitimate "SyncHost.exe" process and inject shellcode into it to load the ThreatNeedle backdoor. The attack chain also incorporated a one-day vulnerability in the Innorix Agent file transfer solution version 9.2.18.496 for lateral movement. Operation FlashHole continues the prior wave's targeting of South Korea-focused software to breach targets. Where SyncHole exploited Cross EX, FlashHole has been found to abuse Initech's INISAFE CrossWeb EX, another mandatory financial security solution necessary to access online banking and government portals in the country. According to iniLINE's website, the company entered into a strategic alliance with Initech as far back as 2010 to develop CrossWeb. It's currently marketed by Initech as a certificate-based authentication and electronic-signature solution. That said, the Lazarus Group has a long history of abusing this software to meet its goals. In Q3 2021, it was used to deploy a downloader named Racket in connection with a long-running campaign called DeathNote. Operation FlashHole attack flow during initial compromise Between 2022 and 2023, AhnLab also disclosed attacks in which the threat actor exploited a security flaw in the software to distribute DLL malware ("SCSKAppLink.dll") via watering hole attacks, with the DLL payload retrieved from IIS web servers compromised by the threat actor. "The group first hacks Korean websites and modifies the content provided from the site," AhnLab noted in a July 2023 report. "When a system using a vulnerable version of INISAFE CrossWeb EX V6 visits this website via a web browser, the Lazarus malware (SCSKAppLink.dll) is installed from the distribution site through the INISAFECrossWebEXSvc.exe vulnerability." Initial infection chain The findings also come against the backdrop of a joint July 2026 advisory published by the Korea Internet and Security Agency (KISA) and domestic cybersecurity vendors, highlighting the Lazarus Group's exploitation of vulnerabilities in such financial security programs like AnySign4PC to distribute backdoors like Struggle (aka SIGNBT 3.0) and Brandoor (aka COPPERHEDGE) after tricking victims into visiting malicious URLs through spear-phishing and watering hole techniques. "The attackers induced targets to access malicious URLs through various methods, including watering hole and spear-phishing attacks, and then exploited the vulnerabilities to ultimately install backdoor malware," AhnLab said, calling the campaign Operation Double Barrel. The precise initial access vector for FlashHole is unclear, but signs point to malicious websites hosted on GitHub pages, one version of which hosted the résumé of a senior network appliance developer along with a profile photo likely generated using artificial intelligence (AI). Expanded infection chain after gaining persistence It's suspected that targets are sent spear-phishing emails containing links to the malicious site, visiting which triggers an infection sequence involving CrossWeb EX to launch the legitimate Windows binary "fsquirt.exe," which is then used to launch a malicious DLL called TechHub via DLL sideloading. "The infection chain is rather complex and reveals the Lazarus Group's advanced operational techniques on targeted hosts," Kaspersky said. "These techniques conceal their malicious payloads, intent, and their sophisticated malware delivery framework." "Significantly, the execution chain below exists only in memory during the initial infiltration, highlighting the attackers' considerable efforts to hide the initial compromise." TechHub, for its part, downloads from GitHub a malware called TouchHub, which leverages a DLL sideloading a second to launch a rogue DLL payload dubbed TOUCHSHIFT ("mscoree.dll") for setting up persistence by kicking off the in‑memory execution of another TechHub instance. Overlaps between Lazarus Group Attacks This second TechHub instance retrieves another malware family known as ClientHub to download and load LPEClient into memory. LPEClient serves as a conduit for Cubridge, the orchestration component of the malware framework designed to fetch various plugins, modules, and tools. Additional details about the malware toolset is as follows - TechHub, an advanced version of the CLOUDBURST and NickelLoader downloader that communicates with GitHub to fetch additional payloads like TouchHub and ClientHub, as well as collect information about the device and its running processes. Cubridge, an improved version of SIDESHOW and LightlessCan capable of communicating with a command-and-control (C2) server and downloading reusable plugins, DLL utilities for one-off tasks, and additional modules to expand its functionality, thereby allowing it to gather comprehensive system information, run commands, and steal files and web browser data. It's also assessed to be an advanced version of CookiePlus. TouchHub, a parent installer for TouchShift. TouchShift, a malware dropper capable of delivering keyloggers, screenshot utilities, and backdoors. ClientHub, a previously undocumented backdoor that comes in two versions: one that communicates with an attacker controlled server, using HTTPS and another that interacts with the Dropbox API. The end goal of the malware is to deploy additional plugins and DLLs. The plugins allow the malware to create ZIP archives, collect files matching a search pattern, delete specific files, and monitor local drive changes and return the collected status information. LPEClient, a longstanding victim profiling and payload delivery tool used since 2019. In August 2026, Check Point revealed that LPEClient was deployed following the zero-day exploitation of CVE-2026-68820, a privilege escalation flaw affecting Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock, to deploy the FudModule rootkit. What's notable about the latest version of the malware is that it uses ML-KEM-1024, a post-quantum cryptographic algorithm, to establish an encrypted connection with the attackers' server before downloading and running additional malware directly in memory. "Operation FlashHole is the latest wave in the broader Cascade Hole campaign, which involves the use of South Korean software as a potential entry point to deliver malware targeting the country," Kaspersky said. The cybersecurity company said the emergence of Operation FlashHole coincided with a fresh wave of attacks targeting various South Korean organizations using the COPPERHEDGE backdoor. In at least one case, the backdoor infection is said to have resulted in the exfiltration of data to a dark web leak site named ULOSE, in a manner similar to Gunra ransomware attacks directed against South Korean entities around the same time. "Lazarus continues to expand its operations, launches new campaigns while introducing new tools and reworking familiar ones to meet its needs," Ryu said in a statement shared with The Hacker News. "What deserves closer attention is Lazarus’s adoption of cryptography designed to withstand future quantum threats. Our findings trace its use back to at least September 2024, showing that these capabilities were already protecting the group’s malware communications more than a year before this disclosure."

fawnj9.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 27, 2026Malware / Cybercrime A criminal using the Amadey malware can no longer access or steal data from 180,000 infected computers around the world, including some in Australia, the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) says. The agency's operators gained access to the criminal's operation's backend and cut it off from those computers. "The next steps that we took were to disconnect that Amadey controller from all those victims," Tauri Gregory, ASD's acting deputy director-general of intelligence, told ABC News in an interview published on October 27. ASD is Australia's foreign signals intelligence and cyber security agency. Its offensive cyber operations need explicit approval from the Australian government and can disrupt cybercriminals overseas by disabling their infrastructure. Amadey was sold to criminals as a service in 2018, according to ESET's analysis of Amadey. Each buyer runs its own control panel on its own servers. Computers infected with Amadey check in with their buyer's command-and-control (C2) server and carry out its orders. Amadey's main job is to install more malware, such as the StealC infostealer. It can also steal credentials and give the buyer remote access to the machine. The most common ways Amadey reached computers were fake software updates, cracked software installers, and other malware loaders. The criminal's Amadey operation was one of many. In its tracking, ESET identified 53 separate Amadey botnets that did not share infrastructure. Disconnecting a controller from its victims also does not undo earlier theft. Credentials stolen by infostealers can sit unused for months before attackers use them, according to Microsoft's analysis. A stolen session cookie can allow an attacker to bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA). ASD's annual cyber threat report, published on October 27, does not describe the operation. Amadey's infrastructure was also disrupted in June by Operation Endgame, an international law enforcement operation that works with private partners. Between June 15 and 19, the operation targeted servers associated with Amadey, StealC, and the SocGholish malware. Australia is one of nine countries whose law enforcement and judicial authorities run Operation Endgame together, according to Europol's June announcement. It was not on Europol's list of countries that took part in the June action week, and the announcement does not mention ASD. In a separate case, ASD said it received a tip that 5 terabytes of data stolen from a business were for sale. The business did not know it had been hacked. The data included business documents, personal data, and login credentials and passwords. The agency broke in and destroyed the data before it could be sold. The destroyed files included an estimated 4.8 million stolen from Australians and hundreds of thousands taken from victims in other countries.

cospwn.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 27, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Data Security OpenAI's compaction feature, which shrinks a long conversation to save space, could be turned into a way to copy a model's hidden reasoning out in plain text, security firm Xint has shown. OpenAI's reasoning models work through a problem before answering, and the service normally returns only the raw reasoning as an encrypted item the user cannot read. The method got past the protections OpenAI added in August against this kind of reasoning theft. OpenAI confirmed the problem and fixed it on October 23, according to Xint. Xint ran the technique against gpt-5.6-sol, one of OpenAI's reasoning models, using math and algorithm puzzles its researchers wrote themselves. The reasoning it pulled out came from those same requests, and Xint did not claim the method could reach another user's reasoning. Xint says it cannot prove the copied text is word-for-word the model's real reasoning, because it never had the original to compare against. Two cheaper models each repeated the item and produced the same text, which rules out mistakes in the copying step but leaves open the possibility that compaction reworded the text. Compaction is an OpenAI feature that uses a model to squeeze a long conversation into a smaller, encrypted item that carries the context forward. Xint sent a task to gpt-5.6-sol and kept the encrypted reasoning it returned. It then called the compaction step on the same model and told it to copy that reasoning into the compacted item word-for-word, with every space changed to a tab to get past OpenAI's usage-policy filters. Because compaction items can move between models, Xint passed the item to the cheaper gpt-4.1 and gpt-4o models and asked each to repeat its input exactly, which they did. The method worked around a fix OpenAI had already shipped. In August, researchers behind a paper called Stolen Thoughts showed that encrypted reasoning from a strong model could be replayed into a weaker model from the same company, which would then repeat it as plain text. OpenAI and others blocked that cross-model replay soon after. Compaction got past that block, Xint said, because the compaction step runs on the same model that made the reasoning, so it never triggers the cross-model check. The idea built on Xint's earlier work, called GhostCompact, which showed the compaction step can be pushed to run tasks of the attacker's choosing. Xint has published the code in its GitHub repository. The fix was on OpenAI's side, so developers who build on the API do not need to change anything. Xint called it an undisclosed fix and said OpenAI paid the researchers a $6,000 reward. Xint tested only gpt-5.6-sol and did not check whether GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI's newer model, is affected. It is not known whether anyone used the method before OpenAI closed it. Xint also argued that fixing this one path may not be enough because, in its view, any server-side step that reads a model's decrypted reasoning and follows the user's instructions could leak it. OpenAI keeps raw reasoning hidden partly to stop distillation, where one company trains a cheaper model on another's outputs. Raw reasoning makes better training data than the final answer alone, because it shows how the model worked through the problem, which is what makes it worth stealing for a rival. OpenAI said in September that it had disrupted a July campaign that tried to expose its models' hidden reasoning, and linked a core part of it to people associated with China's Moonshot AI. Anthropic and a joint U.S. government advisory have each reported China-based labs targeting the hidden reasoning of American models. None of that is tied to Xint's compaction method, which is a demonstration rather than an attack seen in the wild.

1x3a5c0.text: The Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA) has issued an alert warning of unauthorized remote access to video surveillance systems manufactured by Dahua. "Cases of compromising IP cameras and DVRs with access to the video stream, changing the device configuration and creating third-party accounts have been recorded," the State Special Communications Service of Ukraine (SSSCIP) said in an alert issued last week. The primary initial access vector used in the attacks is via Easy4IP, a peer-to-peer (P2P) platform that allows users to remotely monitor homes or small businesses by connecting their Dahua IP cameras, NVRs, and DVRs via a smartphone app or web browser by scanning a QR code or entering the hardware Serial Number (SN). The agency has warned that the serial numbers have a predictable structure containing a 10-character model prefix that's identical for all units of the same device family and a five-character hexadecimal counter that's incremented almost sequentially (e.g., 7K01F36PCA003E8). This, in turn, allows attackers to guess them at scale through a brute-force attack and identify if they are connected to the cloud without hitting rate limits or lockouts. As a result, all devices with active P2P functionality are at risk even if they cannot be accessed directly via the internet. "The assumption that the serial number is unknown to anyone is not a reason to consider the device secure," CERT-UA said. Authentication barriers are overcome by leveraging weak or known passwords, or by exploiting authentication bypass vulnerabilities in outdated firmware versions, such as CVE-2021-33044 and CVE-2021-33045. CERT-UA has shared the following indicators of compromise associated with the activity - Presence of unknown accounts Unauthorized configuration changes Audit logs containing authentication events using the manufacturer's native protocol (DVRIP) and from a local address (127.0.0.1), a sign of P2P access. To counter the threat, it's advised to disable the P2P feature if not required, avoid exposing them directly to the internet, and keep the software up-to-date. The agency has not disclosed who was targeted, when these infections occurred, how many devices had been infected, or who was responsible for the activity. However, the findings share similarities with two clusters of activity that Hunt.io disclosed as targeting IP cameras in Ukraine and Russia. One of the campaigns, attributed to a Russian-speaking operator, singled out internet-exposed cameras in Ukraine using known Dahua and Hikvision vulnerabilities, ultimately compromising 58 devices. The activity involved the exploitation of the following flaws by integrating Ingram, a publicly available webcam vulnerability scanner - CVE-2017-7921 - An authentication bypass vulnerability in Hikvision CVE-2020-25078 - A credential disclosure vulnerability in D-Link CVE-2020-25169 - An unauthenticated information disclosure vulnerability in Reolink CVE-2021-33044 / CVE-2021-33045 - Authentication bypass vulnerabilities in Dahua that allow passwordless login CVE-2021-36260 - An unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in Hikvision. In parallel, the threat actor is also said to have undertaken scanning and exploitation of TP-Link and MikroTik routers and cameras using vulnerabilities like CVE-2024-53375 and CVE-2024-57049 across 15 European countries, including Ukraine, Poland, Romania, Moldova, Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia, Bulgaria, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Italy, Spain, the U.K., and Austria. The second campaign, codenamed Operation CameraSwarm and attributed to a lone threat actor, is believed to have compromised over 14,530 Dahua IP cameras between June 17 and July 22, 2026, using a combination of credential brute-force attacks and the exploitation of the CVE-2021-33044-CVE-2021-33045 chain. The attack scans for TCP port 37777, which is the default proprietary management and video streaming port used by Dahua, followed by collecting serial numbers, breaking into those devices by employing the aforementioned two exploitation methods, and then deploying a persistent backdoor account ("p2pwn / p2password") on nearly 2,000 cameras in a manner that can survive password change and a factory reset. "1,923 cameras carry a persistent backdoor account (p2pwn / p2password), installed over RPC after either bypass," Hunt.io noted at the time. "It is stored independently of the admin password and survives a password change and, on most firmware, a factory reset. 283 cameras were reached by serial number alone through Dahua's cloud relay, with no device address and, in most cases, no credentials." In some instances, the attackers have been found to abuse Dahua's cloud relay to reach cameras behind NATs using only their serial numbers. Earlier this year, Dutch intelligence agencies warned that Russian actors are compromising IP cameras across the E.U., NATO states, and Ukraine to conduct systematic digital espionage operations and acquire military intelligence. "This actor performs automated analysis of imagery through image recognition software to conduct targeted searches for military vehicles and the military cargo they are transporting," the July 2026 bulletin said. "This provides the actor with, among other things, relevant military data, such as E.U. and NATO military transport routes, weapon deliveries to Ukraine, and the locations of Ukrainian military personnel. The information from IP cameras in Ukraine is used in attempts to neutralize Ukrainian military personnel and to destroy their military material."

9gjiyy.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 27, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Monday confirmed active exploitation of the recently patched PHP2Shell flaws by adding them to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. The PHP vulnerabilities, both rated 9.2 on the CVSS scoring system, facilitate unauthenticated remote code execution on affected deployments - CVE-2026-109618 - An out-of-memory corruption vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution. CVE-2026-109619 - A stale internal request-state vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution. The addition of the two flaws to the KEV catalog comes after Adel Karimi, detection and response lead at Perplexity, confirmed successful instances of remote code execution against honeypot systems on October 24, 2026. "This is now confirmed RCE with usable memory disclosure, not just a crash followed by a suspicious process," Karimi said. "The response delivered an 800 KiB decoded cookie dump, and a function address derived from that dump using the public exploit's offsets appears in the subsequent execution payload." "The evidence demonstrates this chain on the intentionally favorable single-worker mod_php profile; it is not a measurement of exploit reliability on other worker counts, PHP builds, or applications." The issues have been addressed in PHP versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35 released on October 21, 2026. Federal agencies have time until October 29, 2026, to apply the necessary fixes. PHP, short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor, is a server-side scripting language used in roughly 70% of all websites on the internet. According to estimates shared by Censys, more than 32.51 million PHP services are still running an affected version. The severity of the vulnerabilities has prompted numerous advisories from software and security vendors and government agencies across the world, including - ABB Arista Networks Belden Broadcom Canon Citrix Craft CMS Dell Dormakaba Drupal ExpressionEngine F5 Hikvision HP HPE Hitachi Energy HMS Networks Huawei IBM Ivanti Johnson Controls Mitel Moxa NETGEAR October CMS Okta QNAP Rockwell Automation Ruckus Wireless Salesforce Schneider Electric Siemens (1), (2) SonicWall Splunk Synology Veeam Wibu-Systems WordPress As of October 26, 2026, the PHP Foundation also released Windows builds 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1 and 8.2.35-1 to address CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the Brotli decoder library that could also result in privilege escalation and unauthenticated remote code execution. The vulnerability, also known as Broccoli2Shell, HTTP2Shell, and Node2Shell, affects Brotli versions 1.0.3 through 1.0.9, 1.1.0, and 1.2.0. It has been patched in versions 1.0.10, 1.1.1, and 1.2.1, along with other projects that include the C library, including Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, .NET, and Python. "In PHP Windows builds, the vulnerable decoder can be reached through the cURL extension when automatic HTTP response decompression is enabled," the PHP Foundation said. "This is disabled by default in cURL, but applications and HTTP client libraries can enable it."

e9bla9.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 26, 2026Malware / Web Security An unknown threat actor has infected 953 online stores, most of them running Magento, as part of a long-running campaign active since July 2025. According to Dutch e-commerce security company Sansec, the activity is designed to add a small piece of code to the store's pages that, when visited by unsuspecting users, serves malicious JavaScript loader code through Magento CMS blocks. "When you visit, that code makes your browser ask the group's server what to do next," Sansec said. "The server first checks whether you are a real shopper or a security scanner, so scanners get nothing." No less than five distinct domains have been observed over time in connection with the campaign - manulfie[.]click, first seen in July 2025 neswnsssn[.]click, first seen in December 2025 lanhd6549tdhse[.]top, first seen in March 2026 additionalver[.]com, first seen in June 2026 deepveindrilling[.]com, first seen in October 2026 Sansec said it found deepveindrilling[.]com in the CMS blocks of 83 online stores since the domain was registered on October 6, 2026. The latest JavaScript loader domain is hosted behind Cloudflare and only responds to script requests from real visitors of infected stores. The loader is staged within Magento's cms_block database table, which is used to render static content into storefront pages. The ultimate objective of the attack is to launch the attack-controlled code when the CMS block is rendered after a shopper opens the compromised website. While Sansec does not disclose whether the threat actor modifies an existing CMS block (such as header, footer, or promotional banner) or creates a new block, the attacker can adopt either of the approaches to run the loader. Two different versions of the loader have been spotted. In one version, the external JavaScript loaded from the attacker's domain stores the payload in the browser's localStorage. This causes the stashed code to be run again on subsequent visits, even if the external domain becomes unavailable. The second version expands on this behavior by incorporating browser fingerprinting checks to filter out bots and security scanners, while ensuring that only real shoppers are exposed to the malicious code. The exact nature of the final payload remains unknown. Early iterations of the campaign have also been observed using Keitaro, an advertising tracker and analytics platform, as a traffic distribution system (TDS), to route visitors to different responses – i.e., return a payload, a redirect or nothing – based on their characteristics. Sansec said requesting the additionalver[.]com script as a Windows desktop visitor returned as response "QWE=123;," which does nothing apart from setting a cookie that marks the visitor for 24 hours. The deepveindrilling[.]com domain, on the other hand, drops the Keitaro component and integrates the bot-filtering logic into the loader itself. As for the initial access vector, 471 Magento stores are estimated to have been injected with the loader through the PolyShell (aka CVE-2026-48356) vulnerability. Another 102 stores saw files uploaded through the PolyShell or SessionReaper (aka CVE-2025-54236) vulnerabilities. "One store on Magento 2.4.7-p1 had PolyShell webshells disguised as PNG images in pub/media/custom_options/quote/, next to the additionalver.com loader in a CMS block," Sansec said. "The block switched to deepveindrilling[.]com on October 7. The store still lacks APSB26-73, Adobe's PolyShell fix for supported release lines." In another case, an e-commerce store running Magento 2.4.7-p10 with no missing core patches was compromised to add a rogue administrator account and then use it to inject the code. Site owners are advised to audit their sites for suspicious accounts and unexpected CMS blocks in the cms_block and cms_page tables. It's also advised to keep the sites up-to-date and enforce strong passwords. The disclosure comes against the backdrop of PHP2Shell, a set of two critical vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) that have witnessed widespread exploitation attempts following their disclosure last week. However, Perplexity researcher Adel Karimi has recorded what appears to be the first in-the-wild successful exploitation of the vulnerabilities to run shell commands on honeypot servers. These commands have been observed using wget, curl, or PHP CLI to fetch additional payloads from a remote server ("162.35.99[.]94:80").No downloaded second-stage artifacts have been observed so far.

1s77uzf.text: Swati KhandelwalOct 26, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security PHP has rebuilt its official Windows packages for PHP 8.2 through 8.5 to fix CVE-2026-111497, a flaw in the Brotli compression library that the packages include. The flaw can let an attacker corrupt memory and potentially run code. PHP says the flaw can be reached through the cURL extension when the extension decompresses HTTP responses automatically. cURL leaves that off by default, but applications and HTTP client libraries can turn it on. The rebuilt packages, numbered 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1 and 8.2.35-1, come five days after the October 21 releases that fixed the two PHP2Shell remote code execution flaws. They use the same PHP source, so those fixes stay in place, and they now include Brotli 1.2.1, the fixed version. PHP publishes a software bill of materials, a list of the components inside, with each package. For last week's x64 Non Thread Safe builds of all four versions, those lists show Brotli 1.2.0, one of the affected versions. PHP advises Windows users to install the new builds from its downloads page. Because the PHP version itself is unchanged, php -v shows the same number before and after. The -1 in the file name, as in php-8.5.12-1-nts-Win32-vs17-x64.zip, and the SHA-256 hash listed on the downloads page identify the new build. Automatic decompression means cURL asks the server for a compressed response and unpacks it. In PHP code, the CURLOPT_ENCODING option turns it on, and an empty value accepts every format cURL supports. Guzzle, a PHP HTTP client library, sets that empty value by default for requests it sends through cURL, according to the code in its 7.16.1 release and in 8.3.1. Based on that code and PHP's own description, an application that keeps Guzzle's default settings meets the condition for reaching the flaw on last week's Windows builds. The Hacker News has not tested this on a Windows system. An attack would come as a crafted compressed response from a server that the PHP application contacts. Google rates the flaw 9.2 out of 10, or Critical, on the CVSS 4.0 scale. Red Hat rates it 8.1, or Important, on the CVSS 3.1 scale. Imperva researchers ran code through the flaw on one official Node.js build, and it took them several attempts. PHP's notice does not mention any attacks. CISA's assessment of October 23 recorded no exploitation, and the flaw was not in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of that day's update. Researchers at OpenAI found the flaw. Google fixed it in Brotli 1.2.1, 1.1.1 and 1.0.10 when it was first disclosed on October 21. Node.js, Bun and other software that ships its own copy of Brotli have also released fixes. PHP's notice offers no workaround for systems that cannot be updated yet. OpenAI advises turning off automatic Brotli decompression in HTTP clients until the update is installed, and warns that removing br, Brotli's name in the Accept-Encoding header, "alone does not stop a server from sending it." In PHP code, following that advice means not setting CURLOPT_ENCODING, because cURL does not decompress responses without it. In Guzzle, it means setting the decode_content request option to false, which stops all automatic decoding, so gzip responses also arrive compressed.

15myic.text: Cybersecurity researchers are calling attention to what they say is a "recurring social engineering pattern" across hundreds of cases in which threat actors use Microsoft Teams' external chat creation feature to conduct impersonation scams or to deliver malware. "A consistent pattern of attacker behavior has emerged across these incidents: the use of the same throwaway tenants, the same 'IT Support (Internal)' display names, the same remote-access tools, and increasingly, the same payload domains," Arctic Wolf Labs said in a report shared with The Hacker News. The attacks consistently employ IT-themed display names or friendly-sounding first names to subvert external-user warnings in Teams. These messages originate from Teams identities established through newly created or acquired Microsoft 365 tenants. Nearly 30–40% of the cases investigated by the cybersecurity company involve the use of *.onmicrosoft[.]com, a permanent fallback domain automatically generated by Microsoft when a Microsoft 365 tenant is created. These domains masquerade as IT infrastructure, opting for a help desk- or support-themed word as the tenant name to increase their credibility - helpdeskteam365.onmicrosoft[.]com itendpoint365.onmicrosoft[.]com itcoreportal.onmicrosoft[.]com itadmin922.onmicrosoft[.]com corporateitservicellc.onmicrosoft[.]com As observed in many cases before, these Teams sessions are preceded by mail bombing, where the victim's inbox is flooded with hundreds of newsletter or subscription confirmations in a short span of time. The approach is designed to induce a false sense of urgency, with the Teams IT support message arriving soon after to help resolve the problem. Some of the display names observed by Arctic Wolf across different cases are listed below - Help Desk IT Support HelpDesk Manager IT Service Desk – Liam / IT Service Desk (Liam) IT Service Desk – Matt / IT Service Desk – Scott IT Support – Christopher Thomas HelpDesk Supervisor Enterprise IT & Security (Internal) IT Tech Support Internal Business IT Solutions & Support (Internal) Maintenance Service IT-Representative IT/Help Desk In recent iterations, the attackers have been observed adding the target organization's domain or company name in their display name to lend the messages additional legitimacy. "We also observed a recent shift toward paid top-level domains (TLDs) for tenant creation," Arctic Wolf said. "Of the paid domains we identified in these types of scams over the past few months, approximately 50 percent of fake identities used the .top TLD, around 40 percent used a standard .com domain, and just over five percent used multi-level domains such as .com.pl, .com.vn, and .com.br." The activity aligns with that of STAC4749, has a history of creating IT-themed cloud domains under the ".top" TLD and leveraging plausible employee usernames to make the accounts appear authentic. These attacks have led to the deployment of Chaos ransomware, according to Sophos. The attacks specifically go after organizations where external access is enabled. This also involves an element of vishing to trick victims to granting them hands-on-keyboard access through a legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tool like Quick Assist, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect (ConnectWise), TeamViewer, Atera, Zoho Assist, NetSupport, and LogMeIn. The remote access is abused to conduct reconnaissance, deliver additional payloads like the GoGRPC backdoor, facilitate lateral movement to domain controllers, and deploy additional RMM tools like Level for redundancy, before exfiltrating sensitive data and dropping the ransomware binary. "In a subset of cases, attackers leveraged Microsoft's notes," Arctic Wolf said. "Attackers generally avoid pasting a URL directly into Teams, which would trigger Safe Links / ZAP scanning, and instead navigate to the payload themselves during the remote session. Consequently, endpoint and identity telemetry are essential monitoring surfaces alongside message scanning.' In one case identified by the cybersecurity vendor, the threat actor is said to have instructed the user to run a PowerShell command to download a file and then launch it. The PowerShell command is designed to download an MSI installer from Microsoft Azure Blob Storage. When the victim runs the installer, it launches a PowerShell script responsible for extracting and executing a Python implant embedded within it. The backdoor then runs another MSI transaction that issues LDAP queries to Active Directory for all computer and user objects and then transmits the information to an external server. "External Microsoft Teams chat has become an effective initial-access vector because it exploits trust rather than a software vulnerability," Arctic Wolf said. "Across the activity examined, attackers combined email bombing, convincing IT-support impersonation, newly created tenants and domains, and rapid social engineering to move victims from a seemingly routine chat to remote access, payload execution, and, in some cases, broader compromise."

1newb1g.text: This2Shell, That2Shell, Everything2Shell. That's pretty much how the last week went. Critical bugs that let attackers run code remotely are showing up everywhere. Hackers are scanning for targets, some flaws are already being used in attacks, and security teams have more urgent patches than they can keep up with. And that's not even the full story. A leaked key led to a software supply-chain attack. AI agents are being tricked into following harmful instructions. Old bugs are still being used to break into systems, and some attacks are so simple it's hard to believe they still work. Some websites even went offline to avoid taking chances. It's been a rough week for anyone trying to keep systems safe. Here's what happened. ⚡ Threat of the Week PHP2Shell Flaws Puts Organizations on Alert — The PHP Foundation released patches for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, that could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. The security flaws have been codenamed PHP2Shell. Since public disclosure, the shortcomings have witnessed widespread scanning efforts, with Cloudflare stating it detected millions of exploitation attempts after public disclosure. To date, no successful exploitation has been observed. The severity of the flaws, coupled with the ubiquity of PHP on the web, prompted several websites to go offline as a precautionary measure. 🔔 Top News eMudhra Exits TLS Certificate Market After Compromise of Weak Private keys — Eight intermediate CA certificates from Indian digital security firm eMudhra were found to use ridiculously weak private keys, potentially allowing bad actors to break them and potentially issue trusted certificates for arbitrary domains. Major web browsers stepped in to block the affected CAs. "On 19 October 2026, Apple began blocking these 12 certificates on Apple devices," Apple said. "Updates to certificate configuration data are sent to devices automatically and as needed, so you don't need to install a software update to get this change. Apple is making additional updates to this block, which will also be delivered automatically. On 23 October 2026, Apple also began blocking the emSign ECC Root CA - G3." Python has also released updated versions of the packages certifi, pip, uv, sigstore, conda, and pixi to remove the emSign root CA certificate from CA bundles. The development prompted eMudhra to exit the certificate-issuing business. Critical Flaw in Brotli Fixed — A severe vulnerability has been addressed in Google's Brotli decoder library (CVE-2026-111497) that could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution. The flaw, also called Node2Shell and HTTP2Shell, has also been addressed in other popular libraries that rely on Brotli, including libbrotli, Python, C++, Node.js, Bun, Envoy, and Istio. The disclosure comes as Ruby released versions 4.0.9, 3.4.12, and 3.3.13 to address several bugs in Ruby's regular expression engine, Onigmo (CVE-2026-89078, CVE-2026-93577, CVE-2026-97229, and CVE-2026-110264) that could be used for remote code execution on GitLab servers. Two CVSS 9.0 Linux KSMBD RCE Flaws Disclosed Ahead of Fixes — Linux servers running KSMBD, the kernel's built-in SMB server, are exposed to two publicly reported remote code execution flaws tracked as ZDI-CAN-33774 and ZDI-CAN-33549, along with a local privilege escalation flaw referred to as ZDI-CAN-33367. None of the vulnerabilities has been assigned a CVE ID, and no in-the-wild exploitation has been reported. "Affected organizations should immediately restrict unprivileged user namespaces and enforce RuntimeDefault seccomp where they can, find out whether ksmbd is running anywhere in their estate, and patch ZDI-CAN-33367 the day their distribution ships the fix," Sysdig said. Plex2Shell Flaws Exploited in the Wild — Four vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server, CVE-2026-96652, CVE-2026-96654, CVE-2026-96655, and CVE-2026-96656, are being chained into an exploit called Plex2Shell to deliver cryptocurrency miners and proxy software. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added all four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog. Railway Warns of Targeted Campaign — Railway said it became aware of a "sustained and targeted campaign" to breach its infrastructure on October 20, 2026, at 7:53 p.m. UTC with an aim to conduct distillation attacks. "Early investigations tell us this attack was attempting to obtain AI provider API keys to perform distillation attacks," it said. "Initial evidence leads us to believe that the malicious actor had access to abliterated models and substantial compute resources which enabled them to perform highly sophisticated exploits against our infrastructure." The developer platform is urging users to revoke and reapply sensitive environment variables stored on Railway prior to October 21, 2026. LiteLLM Leaked Master Key Leads to Supply Chain Attack — LiteLLM revealed that an Agent Platform master key accidentally published to a public GitHub repository in late May 2026 ultimately allowed the threat actor to push a malicious version of the popular Python package. The files bundled with LiteLLM version 1.107.0 are engineered to execute automatically when Python starts, even if an application did not import LiteLLM. The malware features two execution paths: a credential harvesting module that targets authentication material across developer tools, AI applications, cloud environments, and web browsers, and a Unix-oriented backdoor that's launched as a background process to fetch and execute arbitrary code supplied by the attacker every one hour. The malware attempts to set up a LaunchAgent for persistence, and then encrypts files in the user's Downloads folder. "Heartbreaker is unlikely to pose a major real-world threat in its current form," Wardle said. "It only targets files under ~/Downloads, lacks awareness of macOS privacy protections, embeds a universal recovery key, depends on a now-unavailable build framework, and performs an exceptionally noisy Rust installation and compilation workflow. Its disabled 'Decrypt Files' button does not actually recover anything, either. Heartbreaker demonstrates an unusual approach to metamorphism on macOS. Rather than decrypting or rewriting its machine code in memory, it carries its own Rust source, transforms that source, invokes the native build toolchain, and attempts to replace itself with the result. Because each generation embeds its newly transformed source, the design can – in principle – continue across executions." "An AGENTS.md is a file a coding agent is built to trust and obey, and ~/Downloads is the one folder a website can drop a file into with no click and no permission," Forever Security said. "Together, that lets the web plant orders your own agent carries out. Markdown is the new executable. The planted file makes the agent rewrite its own configuration. From there it can install malware (remote code execution) or hand over its own login token (account takeover)." It's unclear how the malicious instructions file ended up on the target's Downloads folder, although it's possible that threat actors could trick a user into downloading it by simply visiting a specially crafted page. Signal messages that authorities accessed when they apprehended ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap in the Netherlands reportedly show frequent contact with Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky and at least one executive at a U.S. consulting firm, who sometimes knew about new victims before the victims themselves, citing an unnamed source. "The Dutch hacker's chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files," Krebs said. The U.S. Army is allegedly developing a program to deploy autonomous AI agents that can navigate digital and network infrastructures of its adversaries, and "neutralize" them, The Intercept reported. The nascent program, codenamed ECHOTRIBBLE, is primarily focused on offensive missions with the goal of "disabling the threat completely or temporarily, deleting the threat from the target." In addition, the system "would function almost like a computer worm, silently navigating a foreign network and hopping from device to device until it finds the Army's quarry, hitting targets in the cloud as well as those on “air-gapped” systems that are disconnected from networks entirely. Once its task is complete, ECHOTRIBBLE's agents would effectively self-destruct, ideally without having been noticed by the target at all." It's described as a "targeted blackhole attack that analyzes the VPN traffic metadata (sizes, direction, timing of packets) to identify narrow time windows, called critical superperiods, during which the site-SCADA traffic would likely contain highly critical commands or data." An attacker with control over a router on the network path could examine the size, direction, and timing of VPN-encrypted packets to predict when critical commands or data are likely to be exchanged, and then deliver malicious payloads during those time periods. "Post-analysis, in a subsequent operational cycle, ICS-Sniper drops a small set of payload-carrying packets in the critical superperiods to disrupt the ICS's operations," the study said. In tests on emulated versions of a Secure Water Treatment (SWaT) plant testbed, the attack delayed the start of clean water pumping by about 15 minutes and kept a valve open more than nine minutes longer than intended. A lifetime subscription costs $500, but cracked versions of the program are said to be shared by multiple actors. Campaigns using the malware have targeted the U.K., Germany, France, Spain, Italy, and the Netherlands. GhostKernel has also been observed advertising BTMob v4.0, an Android trojan, on their Telegram channel.
