1mh4mag.text: Moldova is investigating whether foreign state actors were involved in a major cyberattack on its government systems that exposed sensitive personal information and disrupted dozens of public services, the country's prime minister said Wednesday. Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said the incident may be part of a broader campaign targeting both citizens' personal data and government digital infrastructure, according to local media reports. "Our country is the target of coordinated and large-scale cyberattacks. We are not talking about an isolated incident," Tofan said, adding that authorities were examining the possible involvement of foreign state actors. Moldova has not publicly attributed the attack to any country or hacking group. Tofan's statement came a day after Moldova's Electronic Governance Agency (AGE) disclosed that hackers had exploited vulnerabilities in government services to extract large volumes of personal information between October 19 and 23. The attackers made approximately 11 million requests to access data through government services. Preliminary findings indicate that information linked to about 750,000 identification numbers was extracted, although not every affected individual had all categories of personal data exposed. The compromised information may include names, dates and places of birth, family relationships, health insurance status, social benefits, pensions, disability records, driver's licenses, photographs and vehicle ownership details. Financial information, including bank account numbers, tax debts and government payment histories, may also have been accessed, according to the agency. Authorities said bank card information was not compromised and investigators had found no evidence that attackers had altered official government records. According to the agency, the hackers exploited vulnerabilities in services that did not require authentication and used the information they obtained to extract additional data from interconnected government systems. In response, authorities inspected 82 digital public services and temporarily disconnected those considered vulnerable, along with more than 30 government information systems and administrative panels. The disruptions affected a range of public services, including online applications for construction permits, veterinary transport authorizations, medicine imports and food safety registrations, according to local media reports. Most affected services have since been secured, and authorities are gradually restoring access following additional security checks, the agency said. Authorities said they blocked unauthorized access on October 23 but detected additional attempts to breach government services on Sunday and Tuesday. Both attempts were unsuccessful. The government warned that stolen information could be used in fraud schemes, including attempts to impersonate banks or public institutions to obtain passwords, authentication codes or money. Government spokesperson Dumitru Ciorici said the incident could be part of a broader campaign of hybrid attacks against Moldova. The country of approximately 2.4 million people, which borders Ukraine and Romania, has faced repeated cyberattacks and influence operations since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Moldovan authorities have previously accused Russia of conducting destabilization campaigns aimed at undermining state institutions and public confidence in the country's pro-European government under President Maia Sandu. 1maddko.text: Chinese state-sponsored hacking group Volt Typhoon has been using a framework that relies on rotating chains of connected devices compromised on demand, including for zero-day attacks targeting high-value systems. The framework has been dubbed Silent Train because the threat actor uses it against select targets, cleans it up after each operation, and refreshes it continuously. Researchers at Black Lotus Labs, the threat research division of communications company Lumen, have been tracking Silent Train for three years and confirmed that Volt Typhoon exploited at least four zero-day vulnerabilities in attacks targeting edge and management infrastructure. Targets include telecommunication firms, government agencies, defense contractors, educational institutes, utilities/critical infrastructure, satellite service providers, IT firms, MSPs, transportation, aviation, and emergency services. Black Lotus Labs’ observations indicate the most targeted regions are California, Texas, and Hawaii, suggesting a focus on Indo-Pacific matters. Victims map Source: Black Lotus Labs Volt Typhoon previously targeted U.S. critical infrastructure, including communications, energy, transportation, and water systems, with CISA warning that it seeks to establish access for potential disruption during a future crisis or conflict. According to the researchers, Silent Train's deployment was partly fueled by the FBI's disruption of KV-Botnet, a botnet that Volt Typhoon used to evade detection when attacking critical infrastructure in the US. Activity comparison over time Source: Black Lotus Labs Silent Train relay network Silent Train is practically a relay infrastructure formed of compromised devices that Volt Typhoon uses to hide the origin of its attacks. The operators route their activity through VPS infrastructure outside the United States, then pass it through hacked devices such as routers that act as intermediate relays before launching attacks. Black Lotus Labs says Intelbras modems served as overseas relays, while Netgear Orbi devices acted as hops in the U.S. Silent Train attack overview Source: Black Lotus Labs The threat actor's use of Silent Train involves exploiting vulnerabilities, stealing credentials, exfiltrating data, and maintaining persistent remote access to compromised systems. By monitoring Silent Train activity, the researchers were able to observe zero-day exploits for the following products: CVE-2026-16812 – VeloCloudOrchestrator CVE-2026-20127 – Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876 – N-able N-central CVE-2024-39717 – Versa Director Quest KACE (suspected zero-day) Compromising these platforms gives threat actors broad administrative control, enabling credential theft, remote access, and reach into downstream customers without the “noisy” lateral movement that might trigger detection. Exploitation timeline Source: Black Lotus Labs “To construct these sessions, its operators exploit exposed web interfaces on SOHO, IoT, and other relay devices, then deploy only the tooling needed to enable chained SSH access through the compromised node,” Black Lotus Labs explains in a report today. “This included temporary SSH services, keys, configuration files, and “live off the land” utilities.” After the session ends, typically in under 8 hours, the threat actors remove all their tooling, keys, and configuration files from the disposable relays. By early 2025, researchers noticed that the framework become hybrid, using disposable relays alongside compromised enterprise systems thaat were retained between one and three months. Black Lotus Labs believes Silent Train was reserved for high-value targets and careful, hands-on operations conducted on China Standard Time (CST) timezone. The use of zero-days against those targets further strengthens the assumption. The researchers recommend strengthening security around centralized management systems, restricting internet access to administrative interfaces, rapidly patching vulnerabilities, and centralizing logs with longer retention. They also advise monitoring for unusual administrative activity, reviewing trusted connections that could expose customer or partner networks, and following CISA and NCSC guidance on Volt Typhoon. mwslnc.text: The British government will consult on how to hold technology companies liable for cyber breaches caused by insecure products — potentially a landmark shift for a country that has for years relied on voluntary codes to encourage software vendors to improve security. The commitment, made in budget documents published on Wednesday, comes amid growing alarm in Westminster over the economic damage caused by cyberattacks. Last year's hack of Jaguar Land Rover alone is estimated to have cost the British economy £1.9 billion ($2.5 billion). According to the budget, the government “will consult next year on how to tackle insecure technology at source and consider where liability for cyber breaches should sit.” The work will build on an ongoing review of product liability law by the Law Commission of England and Wales. Although the pledge occupies just one bullet point in the 166-page document, it marks the first formal pledge by a British government to examine where liability for cyber breaches should sit. Significant questions remain, including which department will lead the consultation, when it will begin and whether ministers envisage a civil liability regime, statutory obligations on vendors, or both. HM Treasury did not respond to a request for comment. One option likely to be considered internally is expanding the Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure (PSTI) Act, which since 2024 has imposed basic security requirements on manufacturers of consumer smart devices. Officials are expected to ensure any new rules are compatible with the European Union’s own software cybersecurity regime, to avoid businesses facing heavy costs to comply with two separate sets of requirements. The move follows years of pressure from Britain's own cybersecurity authorities, particularly Ollie Whitehouse, the chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which is part of the cyber and signals intelligence agency GCHQ. The agency called publicly for a “strategic policy agenda” last year, after efforts to address insecure technology had stalled. Whitehouse had already warned, in a keynote address at the CyberUK conference in Birmingham in 2024, that the technology market was failing to reward companies for building resilient and secure products, while regulation and legislation struggled to keep pace. Last year, he wrote that “the reality is that in 2025, we know how to build secure products and services” but “the business and commercial incentives to encourage adoption and sustainment of secure solutions are not sufficient.” His argument echoed a debate in the United States, where proposals to make software makers liable for flawed code stalled for years amid disagreements over how to define the proper standard of care. The Trump administration has since rolled back several Biden-era secure-software requirements for federal suppliers. The political pressure in Britain intensified last November, when the House of Commons Business and Trade Committee, chaired by Liam Byrne, said a lack of liability for software vendors was among the most pressing issues putting Britain’s economic and national security at risk. It urged ministers to make the NCSC's voluntary software security code of practice legally binding, with penalties for companies that fail to comply. Byrne described the Jaguar Land Rover attack as a “cyber shockwave ripping through our industrial heartlands,” while the committee warned of “a huge increase in the private ownership of public risk.” The government's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, introduced to Parliament that same month and now before the House of Lords, acknowledged some of the market failures identified by the NCSC in its impact assessment, which pointed to the “information asymmetry between vendors and buyers” making it difficult for customers to judge the security of the technologies they purchase. In its current form, the legislation stops short of imposing obligations on software developers, concentrating instead on operators of critical infrastructure and their suppliers. Arguments ahead The European Union’s Cyber Resilience Act allows regulators to fine manufacturers of insecure products up to €15 million or 2.5% of global turnover, whichever is higher, with its main obligations taking effect in December 2027. A separate overhaul of the bloc’s product liability rules, which member states must adopt by December, extends strict liability to software, including defects caused by missing security updates. Attempts in Britain to shift liability onto software vendors are likely to face resistance, with the Business Software Alliance — whose members include Microsoft, Oracle and Amazon Web Services — having lobbied against such measures and argued that they would stifle innovation. The proposals could also create friction with the United States, where the world’s largest technology vendors are based, and where successive administrations have regarded overseas regulatory efforts with suspicion when they appear to constrain the sector's commercial success. In Britain, the Law Commission consultation referenced in the budget opened on October 8 and runs until January 14. It proposes broadening the definition of a “product” under the Consumer Protection Act 1987 to include software and AI systems, which currently sit in a legal gray area because the law was written for physical goods. That review is sponsored by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, but responsibility for national cybersecurity policy now lies with the Department for Culture, Media and Sport. The country’s cyber minister, Baroness Lloyd, holds posts in both departments, as Recorded Future News previously reported. £154 million for AI cyber defenses Alongside the liability consultation, the budget commits £154 million ($205 million) in new funding for cyber defenses, much of which the Treasury had announced ahead of Wednesday's statement. The largest allocation is £70 million ($93 million) for a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre at the NCSC. The centre will, according to the budget, use artificial intelligence to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the wider economy. The NCSC already scans internet-connected devices hosted in Britain, alerting organizations to exposed or vulnerable systems through its Early Warning and Proactive Notifications services. The budget does not explain how NERV will differ from those existing operations, and an agency spokesperson declined to comment. A further £60 million ($79 million) will support the first phase of the NCSC’s Cyber Shield, announced in April as “a national scale, sovereign defense capability” that would use agentic AI systems to discover and fix cybersecurity weaknesses across government networks and critical national infrastructure. Remaining funds will be used to strengthen the security of technology across the public sector, including systems operated by local authorities, hospitals and schools. Separately, the government has allocated £40 million ($53 million) to establish a National Agentic Security Unit, tasked with detecting, investigating and responding to rogue AI agents. The budget describes the unit’s ambitions as developing “world-first capabilities to detect and respond to misaligned agentic activity,” but does not identify which agency will host it nor how it will interact with similar projects associated with the NCSC. The AI Security Institute, transferred to the Cabinet Office in July, will receive another £120 million ($159 million) over four years to expand its testing of frontier AI models. The investments follow a week in which critical flaws in PHP, discovered using AI, forced websites offline around the world. The NCSC urged organizations to patch affected systems or consider taking them offline. No previous articleNo new articlesAlexander Martin is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. 1dqjgw0.text: Belarus-linked hackers are increasingly aligning their cyber operations with Russia's interests in Ukraine, the cybersecurity firm ESET said Wednesday. Researchers have observed an "unprecedented operational convergence" between Russian and Belarusian hacking campaigns over the past few months. "We observed increased and more assertive activity from Belarus-aligned threat actors, with their operations increasingly reflecting Russia's intelligence priorities in Ukraine in some areas," researchers said. The most significant development came in late May, when a Belarus-linked hacking group launched a destructive cyberattack against a Ukrainian manufacturing company believed to play an important role in the country's transportation sector. The attack was attributed to GhostWriter, a threat actor linked to Belarusian intelligence services that has previously conducted cyberespionage and influence operations against Ukraine, Poland and other countries in the region. ESET said it was the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned group that its researchers had documented in Europe, marking an escalation from the group's previously observed activities. The hackers used data-wiping malware, which can erase information from compromised systems and disrupt their operations. ESET could not establish whether the malware was intended to cause damage or simply cover the tracks of an espionage operation. Regardless of the hackers' motivation, the attack "sets a precedent" and raises the possibility that other Belarus-aligned state groups could carry out wiper attacks in the near future, researchers said. Although Belarus has not deployed its own troops to fight in Ukraine, it has supported Russia's invasion by allowing Moscow to use its territory to launch military operations and missile strikes. Belarusian hackers have historically focused on espionage and influence operations serving Minsk's own interests, but the latest destructive attack appeared more closely aligned with Russia's wartime priorities, according to ESET. The researchers also identified several other Belarus-linked espionage operations targeting organizations of particular interest to Russia in connection with the war. Researchers suggest that Belarusian hacking groups are increasingly serving as proxies or "force multipliers" for Russia. ESET warned that the trend could lead to closer cooperation between Russian and Belarusian hackers, including the sharing of tools and infrastructure, the outsourcing of targeting operations or even direct collaboration on cyberattacks. North Korea's growing role In addition to Belarus-linked groups, ESET found that North Korean hackers have stepped up their cyberattacks against Ukrainian targets amid growing military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow. The researchers found some overlap between Moscow's and Pyongyang's intelligence interests, particularly regarding Ukraine's rapidly developing drone industry. However, researchers said the evidence of North Korean cyber operations directly supporting Russia's war effort was less definitive than the growing alignment they observed among Belarusian groups. North Korean hackers have nevertheless expanded their targeting of Ukrainian organizations, potentially seeking intelligence and technical expertise that could benefit Pyongyang's own military capabilities. Other cybersecurity researchers have also reported growing North Korean interest in Ukrainian targets. Earlier in October, South Korean cybersecurity firm Genians said the North Korean hacking group Kimsuky had targeted Ukrainian experts in diplomacy, security and international policy. In May 2025, cybersecurity firm Proofpoint reported that North Korean-linked hackers had sent malicious emails to Ukrainian government agencies, potentially seeking intelligence about threats facing North Korean troops deployed alongside Russian forces. 1jtq7xg.text: Sony Network Communications has confirmed a data breach that compromised approximately 2.5 million records containing current and former customers’ personal information. A Sony Group Corporation subsidiary, the company provides telecommunications and technology services, acting as an internet service provider (ISP) in Japan. The breach occurred on October 19 and was detected four days later, when the company shut down the compromised servers and blocked external communication. In an announcement yesterday, the company said that its So-net member database, supporting its internet access service, was accessed by an unauthorized party. The investigation confirmed that a total of 2,585,481 customer records had been exposed, including the following types of information: Full names Phone numbers Email addresses User IDs Dates of birth Gender Internet Connection IDs No banking, payment card, or other account details were exposed. An additional 54,401 email addresses from several email services were also exposed along with account passwords. The company advises users to change their passwords. In the breakdown of exposed records, Sony Network Communications says there are 2,141,986 So-net entries and 443,495 plala (S Course) records. The latter impacts another internet service provider, NTT Docomo, which contracts Sony Network Communications to provide its Docomo Hikari services. NTT Docomo also notified customers about the breach and warned of phishing emails and fake websites impersonating its d POINT Club and a Universal Studios Japan (USJ) campaign, falsely claiming that recipients had won and prompting them to enter personal information to claim tickets. Docomo says the incident affects all current Hikari service clients and those who canceled within the preceding six months. Sony reported the incident to Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission and is investigating its cause and scope. As of October 27, neither company had confirmed misuse of the exposed data in the wild. Since the start of the year, multiple cyberattacks have targeted high-value companies and providers in Japan. One of the most recent is the incident at GMO Internet Group and its Onamae Desktop Cloud service, which suffered a widespread malware attack on customer servers. Telecommunications giant KDDI suffered a breach affecting 12 million customers, and IDC Frontier was targeted by ransomware. Previously, NTT was hit in early 2025 by hackers who gained access to its systems and stole the data of 18,000 corporate customers. The recent rate of data breaches is so unprecedented and threatening that the Japanese government held urgent meetings on Monday to plan its response. ukbasq.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 28, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Espionage Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of what appears to be an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted attack orchestrated by a suspected China-nexus threat actor that has leveraged the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities to breach exposed systems. The activity, which was observed on October 25, 2026, involved an attacker combining PHP2Shell with a kernel privilege escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including three systems in a U.S. government-affiliated environment. "The affected devices run specific versions of a large vendor's firewall software," cybersecurity firm Dream said. "The attacker then launched attacks against Active Directory. The recovered artifacts confirm credential extraction and directory enumeration." The name of the affected vendor was not disclosed, but the Israeli company said it notified the entity. The attack chain essentially brings together two sets of vulnerabilities impacting PHP and the Linux kernel - PHP2Shell, a pair of flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS scores: 9.2) that could result in unauthenticated remote code execution Fragnesia, a Linux kernel local privilege escalation vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-46300 (CVSS score: 7.8) "The implementation we recovered is a custom, non-public build, not a copy of any known public exploit for PHP2Shell," Dream researchers explained. "It follows the same underlying concept but appears to have been independently developed and tailored specifically for the targeted firewall platform." "The vulnerability targets PHP's session.upload_progress mechanism on the firewall's appweb management server. The firewall OS uses PHP 8.0.30 with a high memory limit that enables the memory corruption stages of the attack." The custom weaponization of the PHP2Shell exploit chain, coupled with CVE-2026-46300, is said to have rooted 25 servers across the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea. Artifacts discovered by Dream indicate that the operation started with exploit development in a lab environment before obtaining persistent access to a U.S. government organization's internal Active Directory domain. "Once rooted, the attacker zeroed in on three specific servers in a U.S. government-affiliated environment," the company noted. The links to AI-assisted tooling stem from evidence pointing to the installation of Anthropic's Claude Code in the attack infrastructure, along with the presence of API keys for FOFA and an AI-powered offensive security platform called aiscan configured with large language models (LLMs) from DeepSeek and Kimi. What's more, the code structure, commenting style, and consistency across nearly 40 scripts suggest the use of AI to augment the development process. The entire operation, per Dream, unfolds as follows - Attacker uses FOFA to identify approximately 19,000 internet-facing firewalls with exposed management interfaces worldwide. A custom version scanner is executed to determine which among those devices are online and what operating system version they are running. About 5,000 devices respond with the version information. The attacker filters the servers to those located in the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, and then limits the scope to systems that match newer release branches running PHP 8.0.30. This step yields 240 targets. The target list is fed as input to an automated batch runner that exploits the PHP2Shell-Fragnesia chain, plants a PHP web shell on a publicly accessible directory on the firewall, verifies root access, and logs the target's hostname and IP to a CSV file. This step allows the attacker to gain root access to 24 servers. Two of the successfully compromised systems are identified as belonging to a U.S. government-affiliated organization. One of them crashes shortly after it was rooted on October 23, 2026, at 6:14 p.m. UTC and never comes back online. The attacker carries out a dedicated campaign to successfully root a second system on October 24, 2026, at 10:09 a.m. UTC. The attacker exploits the second system to build a persistent channel into the internal network via a reverse SSH tunnel connecting the compromised firewall back to the operator's infrastructure. At 11:35 a.m. UTC, a third government server is compromised using the same method, the only difference being that this was an internal firewall management server only reachable through the tunnel. The total number of rooted servers reaches 25. The attacker targets Active Directory to decrypt the LDAP service account password, enumerate users, and spray passwords against every user account using organization-themed passwords in an attempt to extract credentials. The operation also attempts to create backdoor Active Directory accounts. It's unclear if the activity allowed the threat actor to successfully find valid credentials or create backdoor accounts. As a result, the full extent of the compromise remains indeterminate. "Since [the] U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea are the four primary strategic adversaries and intelligence targets for Chinese state-aligned cyber operations in the Pacific theater, this indicates potential nation-state adversary efforts," Dream said. "The operation illustrates how an exposed management interface can become a path into an organization's identity infrastructure. The 22 other rooted firewalls remain parked with active web shells. The persistent tunnel into the US government organization is likely still running. And the attacker still has 19,000 fingerprinted targets they can revisit as they develop profiles for additional OS versions." The disclosure comes as the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities have witnessed only limited exploitation in the wild, with threat actors highlighting the challenges in converting a proof-of-concept (PoC) into a reliable attack vector against real targets despite integrating them into their campaigns. "In practice it's unexploitable crap. To exploit real targets you need the offsets from libphp.so, which are unique to every build and impossible to brute-force. You can reproduce it on your own test bench, or if you already have access to the target's file system," a member who goes by the handle c0d3x on the XSS forum said, according to Flare.

cubjns.text: Microsoft again asked Entra ID administrators to migrate users to phishing-resistant methods to avoid sign-in disruptions before it retires SMS and voice authentication in February 2027. This retirement process applies only to Microsoft Entra ID workforce tenant authentication scenarios and not to Azure AD B2C or Microsoft Entra External ID customer identity scenarios. Before Microsoft retires SMS and voice authentication, admins should ensure all users in their organizations use a phishing-resistant method, since they will no longer be able to use them to complete multifactor authentication and log in to their accounts. Admins can choose from passkeys, QR code authentication, FIDO2 security keys, and other Entra ID-supported sign-in methods. "Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication will retire starting February 1, 2027. Complete your migration before rollout begins to avoid interrupting users' sign-in experience," Microsoft said in a Microsoft 365 Message Center update on Tuesday. "SMS and voice are vulnerable to phishing and SIM-swap attacks. Microsoft recommends passkeys for stronger, phishing-resistant protection. You can also migrate to another supported authentication method or retain SMS and voice by configuring a customer-managed telecom provider (CYOT) through the Microsoft Security Store." As Microsoft noted in a previous reminder issued in September, admins with the Authentication Policy Administrator, Global Reader, or Security Reader roles can find users with SMS or voice authentication with the Entra SMS/Voice Policy Scanner PowerShell script. Organizations that must use phone-based authentication have to configure third-party telecom providers through the Microsoft Security Store. plxht2.text: Ravie LakshmananOct 28, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security Threat actors are beginning to probe for a newly patched critical vulnerability in Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS), according to threat intelligence firm Defused Cyber. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-101767 (CVSS score: 9.8) in the Oracle Application Object Library of Oracle E-Business Suite. It was patched by Oracle last week as part of its Critical Patch Update. Security researchers Brandon Peterson, Jimi Sebree, and Noah King of Horizon3.ai have been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw to Oracle on July 24, 2026. "Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767, an unauthenticated SQL injection in EBS's Thin Client Framework servlet that chains to remote code execution, this morning, October 27," Defused Cyber said in an X post. In an advisory for the vulnerability, Horizon3.ai described it as an unauthenticated SQL injection vulnerability that could be chained to achieve remote code execution. "The vulnerability allows an attacker with network access to the affected Thin Client Framework (TCF) servlet to execute SQL as the APPS database user, then run operating system commands as the EBS application account," the cybersecurity company said. Specifically, an attacker can issue a crafted request to the vulnerable TCF servlet at "/OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer" to run SQL with the privileges of the APPS database user and ultimately enable system command execution with the privileges of the EBS application account. Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-101767 can permit an attacker to read or modify application data accessible to APPS and execute commands on the application host. "Depending on the deployment, affected data may include financial, payroll, HR, and procurement records. Operating system access is governed by the permissions of the compromised EBS application account," Horizon3.ai warned. While internet-facing EBS deployments present the most risk, internal EBS systems can also be exploited if an attacker can reach the vulnerable servlet from a compromised system or another accessible network segment. Users are advised to update to the latest version as soon as possible. If immediate patching is not an option, the following workarounds can be applied - Remove /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer, associated with oracle.apps.fnd.tcf.SocketServer, from the EBS URL firewall allowlist. Restrict access to the EBS web tier to trusted networks. Monitor the EBS application host and database for signs of compromise. Horizon3.ai has also shared the below indicators of compromise - Unauthenticated POST requests to /OA_HTML/AppsTCFServer that instantiate the Gantt data-server class (oracle.apps.jtf.gantt.server.GanttDataServer), followed by backend database activity. SQL reconnaissance shortly after unauthenticated web requests (database version, current user, directory objects). Unexpected files in $APPLPTMP and the oracle account spawning /bin/sh via the Concurrent Manager to run OS commands. Vulnerabilities in EBS are a hot target for attackers. Over the past year, two critical flaws in the same product (CVE-2025-61882 and CVE-2026-46817, CVSS scores: 9.8) have come under active exploitation, with the former leveraged by the Cl0p ransomware and extortion crew.

6um3wx.text: Attackers are actively exploiting vulnerabilities across critical network infrastructure, and PHP flaws known as "PHP2Shell" put the web management interfaces of firewalls, VPNs, application delivery controllers, and other appliances at risk. The findings come from Eclypsium's October InfraTrust Pulse, a monthly report tracking security advisories affecting network devices, servers, firmware, chips, and other infrastructure. Between September 18 and October 14, InfraTrust tracked 133 new security advisories across 18 vendors, covering 2,813 vulnerabilities. Of those advisories, 37 were rated critical, five had a maximum CVSS score of 10.0, and 58 could be exploited remotely without authentication. Sixteen newly published advisories included vulnerabilities listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog (KEV) as they were actively exploited. The report also warns that many network appliances, including firewalls, VPN gateways, application delivery controllers, and network-attached storage devices, embed PHP into their management interfaces. Because vendors compile PHP into appliance firmware, customers commonly cannot install the recent PHP security updates themselves and must instead wait for each vendor to release updated firmware. InfraTrust therefore recommends that administrators make sure PHP-backed management interfaces are not exposed to the Internet while waiting for PHP2Shell patches. Critical infrastructure under attack Some of the most serious vulnerabilities affect systems at the edge of enterprise networks or used to manage other infrastructure. Threat actors target these devices because they can provide initial access to corporate environments or serve as a springboard for further attacks. Among the actively exploited flaws highlighted by InfraTrust are: Citrix NetScaler ADC and Gateway: CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 were disclosed on September 27 after attacks had already been observed against unpatched appliances. A separate NetScaler flaw, CVE-2026-88779, affecting appliances configured for SAML was also later added to CISA's KEV catalog after exploitation was detected. Ivanti Connect Secure: CVE-2026-104935 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands on vulnerable VPN gateways. Ivanti said it had exploited a limited number of customers when it published the advisory. CISA later added it to the KEV. Check Point Security Management Server: CVE-2026-93616 allows an unauthenticated attacker to upload and execute scripts on management and logging systems. Check Point Research observed targeted attacks exploiting the flaw on September 12, targeting Spark customers. Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager: CVE-2026-76504 allows an unauthenticated attacker to bypass authentication and gain administrator access to the management API. Cisco became aware of active exploitation in September. Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator: CVE-2026-93952 is a maximum-severity flaw affecting the system used to configure SD-WAN Edge devices. Arista says it is being actively exploited and later disclosed a second, separate exploited vulnerability (CVE-2026-114625) in the same product on October 22. FortiMail: CVE-2026-104286 is a critical path traversal flaw that allows an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files through the web interface. Fortinet confirmed it was exploited in attacks. Cisco Secure Email Gateway: CVE-2026-76519 can allow a malicious email attachment to lead to arbitrary file writes and command execution as root on vulnerable systems. Cisco learned of exploitation in October. F5 BIG-IP APM: CVE-2026-94127 is a critical heap overflow that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on systems configured as OAuth authorization servers. F5 says the vulnerability has been exploited. PAN-OS management interface: Palo Alto Networks reported exploitation of CVE-2026-0322 in attacks on firewalls, allowing an authenticated administrator with network access to execute code as root. php2shell exposes another problem InfraTrust also warns that the recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities expose another weakness in network infrastructure, as many appliances embed PHP directly into their management interfaces. The two PHP flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, allow unauthenticated remote code execution, and the PHP project fixed them on October 21. While most focus on these vulnerabilities has been on websites and web applications written in PHP, PHP is also used for management interfaces of firewalls, application delivery controllers, VPN appliances, and network-attached storage devices. For impacted devices, administrators usually cannot update PHP themselves because vendors compile it directly into the appliance firmware. Instead, customers must wait for each vendor to rebuild and release updated firmware or software containing the patched PHP version. Soon after the disclosure, Palo Alto Networks, F5, NetScaler, Check Point, and QNAP confirmed that some of their products were affected, while they still developed fixes for appliances. The report also highlights a similar issue in other software components that infrastructure vendors bundle into their products. CVE-2026-31431, a Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw known as Copy Fail, has now appeared in 29 advisories across eight vendors, up from 19 advisories from six vendors last month. InfraTrust also found older, exploited vulnerabilities in bundled components, including an Android kernel flaw affecting HP LaserJet Enterprise printers and a 2020 jQuery vulnerability in Dell Data Lakehouse software. InfraTrust recommends that administrators prioritize patching NetScaler and Ivanti Connect Secure because these remote-access gateways can serve as a doorway into corporate networks. Next, it recommends Fortinet's October 22 FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer security updates for internet-facing devices. The report then recommends focusing on Check Point Security Management Server, Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, VeloCloud Orchestrator, FortiMail, Cisco Secure Email Gateway, affected BIG-IP APM systems, and PAN-OS management interfaces. 3hvxub.text: The FBI seized the domain of a “bulletproof” hosting provider accused of facilitating a range of cybercrimes, including money laundering and the distribution of child sexual abuse material. The Justice Department said Tuesday that a court authorized the seizure of virtualine.net — a service operating under names including Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo and Omegatech — which has now been replaced by a splashpage. So-called “bulletproof” hosting providers are specialized criminal businesses that rent critical infrastructure to customers based on the promise they will ignore abuse complaints and law enforcement requests. According to court records, Virtualine explicitly advertised on cybercrime forums, offering hosting for “all illegal/black hat activities,” including phishing, carding and spam. Although the provider claimed to prohibit customers involved in terrorism or child abuse material, prosecutors allege it did not enforce those restrictions. In June 2025, Virtualine boasted on HackForums that it had “ignored more abuse than your last three therapists.” In January, about a month after allegedly providing an IP address to a forum used to sell sexually explicit images of minors, distribute nonconsensual intimate images and advertise account-hacking services, the company was sent complaints from authorities in Germany, Canada and Australia, as well as the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children and a victim’s attorney. Instead of terminating services to the forum, Virtualine helped its operators build another site for uploading and downloading illicit content, according to the Justice Department. The site remained online despite complaints related to sexually explicit images of children. Virtualine accepted bitcoin payments through a service it named “BTC [NO-AML],” referencing anti-money laundering checks. Prosecutors said Virtualine attempted to launder the proceeds to conceal their origin, though some payments were traceable to criminal groups. The FBI’s Washington Field Office led the investigation, assisted by authorities in Germany, the Netherlands and Britain, along with private sector partners OverRIPE and Lumen. The Justice Department did not identify Virtualine’s operators or announce criminal charges at the time of the domain seizure. The seizure follows a series of international actions against bulletproof hosting providers, particularly Russia-linked services accused of supporting ransomware gangs. In February 2025, the U.S., UK and Australia sanctioned Zservers for allegedly supporting the LockBit ransomware gang. Dutch police seized 127 of its servers that same week. The U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned Russia-based Aeza Group in July 2025 for allegedly hosting the BianLian ransomware gang and information-stealing malware. Researchers also linked the provider to the Doppelgänger disinformation campaign. In November, the three countries sanctioned Media Land over alleged ties to the LockBit, BlackSuit and Play ransomware groups. U.S. prosecutors had charged three alleged operators in that case, which they said resulted in about $62 million in victim losses. Dutch authorities arrested two men and seized 800 servers in May during an investigation into infrastructure linked to Stark Industries, an EU-sanctioned provider accused of enabling Russian cyber operations. Investigators said another company took over Stark's infrastructure after sanctions were imposed. The long-term impact of such crackdowns has been questioned. Threat intelligence firm Intel 471 reported in August that disruptions had driven customers to newer providers operated by former resellers, fragmenting the market rather than eliminating demand. 6zay02.text: Attackers have begun probing the Internet for systems unpatched against a recently disclosed critical Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS) vulnerability. Discovered in a core component of EBS's Application Object Library and tracked as CVE-2026-101767, this flaw lets unauthenticated threat actors with HTTP network access take over vulnerable systems in low-complexity attacks. Oracle released security updates to address the issue in its October 2026 Critical Security Patch Update on October 20 and urged customers to patch their systems immediately. "In some instances, it has been reported that attackers have been successful because targeted customers had failed to apply available Oracle patches," it said. While Oracle has not yet tagged CVE-2026-101767 as exploited in the wild, threat intelligence company Defused said on Tuesday that it already spotted threat actors scanning the Internet for vulnerable systems. "Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767, an unauthenticated SQL injection in EBS's Thin Client Framework servlet that chains to remote code execution, this morning, Oct 27," Defused warned. ​Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver now tracks over 670 Internet-exposed Oracle EBS instances, most of them with IP addresses from the United States. However, Shadowserver doesn't indicate how many are honeypots or have already been secured against the CVE-2026-101767 flaw. Internet-exposed Oracle EBS instances (Shadowserver) ​Attackers often target Oracle vulnerabilities because they let them breach enterprise systems on the networks of many Fortune 100 corporations, government organizations, and healthcare networks around the world. ch7gpu.text: Here's a prediction: we're about to see a stellar quarter for application security companies. PHP2Shell is about to become the strongest budget argument application security vendors have had in years. AI helped researchers find two remote code execution vulnerabilities in the language behind 69% of the web, attackers targeted it before the patch shipped, and the pitch writes itself: find more bugs and fix them faster. Enterprises should rethink this idea. Security teams cannot patch at machine speed, but they can reduce what an attacker can reach after exploitation by focusing on identity as the control plane. Beyond the initial exploitation, the ultimate incident severity depends heavily on which service accounts, API keys, cloud roles, and tokens the compromised workload can use and what they can access. From vulnerability to exploitation First, we need to understand just how much faster exploitation is now. The two flaws behind PHP2Shell had been in PHP's code since 2012. Researchers at Calif and Wiz found them in August, with help from OpenAI and Google models, and disclosed them jointly with OpenAI. Amazon saw an exploitation attempt on October 17, four days before disclosure. PHP shipped the patch on October 21, and watchTowr saw exploitation attempts in the wild the same day. Cloudflare observed attack traffic escalating rapidly after disclosure, and on October 26, CISA added both flaws to its list of known exploited vulnerabilities. Exploitation now often starts before disclosure. Unfortunately, things aren't moving as quickly on the remediation side. Verizon's 2026 DBIR states the median time-to-fix of a known exploited vulnerability is 43 days. According to Qualys, the mean remediation time is 21.2 days, and 63% of critical vulnerabilities are still open after a week. All while around 195 new CVEs are published every day. PHP2Shell will take longer than most to clean up. PHP ships inside appliances and hosting control panels that customers can't patch themselves. Moreover, versions 8.1 and older got no official builds. As of October 27, Censys counted 32.5 million internet-facing PHP services still running potentially vulnerable versions, and more than 60 million others that don’t report a version at all. However you look at it, remediation speed will remain slower than the pace of exploitation for the foreseeable future, even when patching itself benefits greatly from AI-driven workflows. Every Agent Needs an Identity Agents now act across your systems with access nobody has reviewed. Token Security’s AI Agent Security finds every agent, links it to an owner, and limits what it can do. Identity-based order to control the chaos of your agentic AI See Token in Action Finding isn't fixing With the exploitation gap widening, it’s tempting to invest everything you can in holding back the tide. But even if an AI-driven scan found 2,000 new zero-day vulnerabilities in your environment tomorrow, that won’t result in a stronger security posture. It will give you a list. Some items will be easy to patch, while others will need more time than your team has. For supported PHP branches, the direct fix was simple: install the updated release. Governments and companies still took their sites offline while they waited for it. Here's another, more optimistic way to look at it. Vulnerabilities lead to exploits, and exploits lead to attacks, but in an enterprise context, the impact of an attack is determined by how far the compromised identities can reach. A shell on a PHP server grants the attacker access to whatever that server can read, from environment variables to cloud keys in config files. PHP2Shell can also leak worker memory, including passwords, tokens, and API keys. An attacker executing code on one host opens a door to a hallway, but the real valuables are usually in locked rooms. And the controls that limit lateral movement don't depend on winning a race against discovery. Finding vulnerabilities is an open-ended process, and limiting the reach of a service account is a quantifiable task. Attackers take the easiest path This approach has limits. If the vulnerability is in the IdP or the secrets manager, lateral movement capabilities come built in. If it's in the database or in the storage provider, the attacker is already where they want to be. So with limited resources, it's tempting to stay vulnerability-first: catalog what the advisories and scanners found, triage it, work down from the top. But cataloging takes weeks, and fixing the most pressing findings takes even longer. The bet here is that the most exploitable holes in your core systems are the ones you'll close first. That bet prioritizes the vulnerability’s severity (the CVSS score) over the blast radius. Attackers aren't looking for the most direct path; they're looking for the easiest path. Taking a leaked credential and moving with it is easier than stringing together zero-days to reach a database directly. October's other headlines show that path. At LiteLLM, attackers used a master key exposed in a public repository to retrieve an unscoped GitHub organization-owner token from an internal agent platform. That identity let them steal two more maintainer tokens, subvert the release workflow, and publish credential-stealing artifacts. Shrink the blast radius first You can’t win the race to patch every server before the attackers arrive, but you can determine what a compromised server is worth to them. Discover and inventory every AI agent and non-human identity and start by securing the ones that reach the most. Assign an owner, scope access to purpose and intent, remove dormant credentials, and continuously govern the identity lifecycle. For AI agents, go further and grant access by intent. That is what it means to treat identity as the control plane. Patching decides how fast you close a hole. Identity decides how much an attacker gets when you can’t. goqrrv.text: A critical 16-year-old flaw in EDK II, the open-source code that most hardware makers use to build UEFI firmware, can allow an attacker to run code on a machine before its operating system loads, but only while the machine is booting over the network. UEFI firmware is the software that runs first when a computer is switched on, before the operating system. An attacker who can reach the machine with a crafted network message during such a network boot can hang the boot, or, with work tailored to the exact firmware build, run their own code before Secure Boot and other startup defenses load. An attacker needs no password and no existing access to the machine, but does need to reach it over the network during the short window when it is booting this way. Red Hat and SUSE, which both ship the affected code, rated the flaw as one an attacker exploits from an adjacent network position rather than across the open internet. TianoCore, the project behind EDK II, published an advisory on October 22 and rated the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-97631, 9.5 out of 10. A code fix exists, but no stable release of EDK II contains it yet, and the advisory still lists no patched version, so most users have nothing to install today. What the Flaw Lets an Attacker Do The flaw is a buffer overflow in EDK II's network-boot code, known as PXE. During a PXE boot, a machine loads its startup image from the network instead of from a local disk. As part of this, the PXE driver listens for ICMP error messages and the small status messages that network devices send back, and copies each one into a fixed 504-byte area of memory. The size checks in that copy are wrong in both the IPv4 and IPv6 versions of the code, so a message longer than 504 bytes spills past the area and overwrites nearby memory with data the attacker chose. To set this off, an attacker only has to send one crafted error message to the machine's address while it is in the middle of a network boot. No password or existing access to the machine is needed. The simple result is a crash: the boot hangs, and the machine fails to start. Getting code to run is much harder and far less reliable. The advisory says that an attacker who knows the exact firmware build can plant a "counterfeit event" that causes the firmware to run the attacker's own code, so an exploit has to be built for a specific build. When code runs, it executes within the firmware, before Secure Boot and other boot-time checks have verified anything. That timing is what makes the flaw serious. Code planted this way runs only once and does not survive a reboot by itself. That single run is still enough to install other code that does start on every boot. Who Is Affected The bug sits in EDK II up to and including edk2-stable202608, the newest stable version, dated August 21. EDK II is the reference code that nearly every UEFI firmware vendor builds on, including the independent BIOS makers AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, as well as Microsoft's hardened fork, Project Mu. The flawed copy loop has been in the code since a commit added in November 2010, The Hacker News found by tracing the project's history. PXE network boot is turned on by default in EDK II's standard build. The flaw does not affect home or office users who boot only from a local disk. It applies to organizations whose machines boot over a network, primarily servers and data center equipment. How many shipping products carry the vulnerable code is not known. Intel told Ars Technica that none of its "commercial products currently under security support" are known to be affected, and that it "does not include the affected EDK2 functionality in its reference code," though an OEM board vendor or system maker could add it. Arm said the flaw "is not directly applicable to Arm's product portfolio." Both companies' own firmware draws on EDK II. Linux distributions also ship the code. Red Hat lists its edk2 package in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9, and 10 as affected and not yet fixed, and SUSE and Debian mark their equivalent packages the same way. AMD, Phoenix Technologies, AMI, Microsoft, and Amazon did not answer the tech news site's questions before publication, and TianoCore did not respond either, so the status of their products remains unclear. Is There a Fix? A fix has been merged into the EDK II source code. It rewrites the faulty copy so an oversized message is cut off at 504 bytes instead of spilling over, and it reached the main development branch on October 15. No stable release of EDK II includes that fix yet. The Hacker News checked the project's release tags on October 28 and found the newest, edk2-stable202608, predates it, and the advisory still lists the patched version as "Not patched currently." Microsoft's Project Mu has already pulled the fix into its release branches, and cut tagged builds on October 26. Even with the fix public in source, a server operator has nothing to install until the maker of their firmware ships a BIOS or UEFI update built from it. That step is at least straightforward, Jesse Michael, a principal researcher at the firmware security firm Eclypsium, told Ars Technica: unlike Secure Boot bypasses such as BootHole and BlackLotus, the flaw "can be fixed with a basic code fix" and does not require certificate or key revocations. Until that update arrives, the advisory lists no workaround. Because the flaw can only be reached during a network boot, operators who do not need PXE can disable it to reduce exposure. Ars also advised watching boot-time network traffic and logs for signs of attempts. How It Became Public The flaw was found by Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes-Mitra of Google, the advisory credits. A coordinated disclosure had been planned for January 2027. That plan was overtaken on September 28, when a pull request to EDK II, signed off by an AMI engineer, publicly described the flaw by its CVE number and included the fix. Once the people who found it saw the post, TianoCore published its advisory on October 22, weeks before the planned date. With the patch public, Ars noted that skilled attackers can study it to determine how the flaw is triggered and build working exploits. There is no sign the flaw has been used in an attack. It was not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of its October 27 update, and no researcher has reported seeing it exploited. The flaw is also not, on its own, a way into a network, Ars Technica reported after putting questions to several firmware researchers. The realistic attacker is an insider, or someone who has already gained a low-level foothold on the local network and wants to dig deeper. "An attacker intent on compromising a nearby endpoint or server could use this bug to hijack program flow at a point where the boot process still has access to sensitive components, like the endpoint's TPM," said HD Moore, the creator of Metasploit and chief research officer at the security firm Dragos, in comments to Ars Technica. "This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access (and it would be even easier in a theft scenario)." It is not the first serious flaw in EDK II's network-boot code. In January 2024, researchers disclosed PixieFail, a set of nine flaws in the same part of EDK II, also reachable during PXE boot. Ars reported that fuzzing projects started after PixieFail to find more bugs in the code did not catch this one.

1121q0e.text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of this decade's defining technologies. From healthcare and finance to manufacturing and education, organizations increasingly rely on AI to automate repetitive tasks, uncover patterns hidden within large datasets, and support faster decision-making. Cybersecurity has experienced a similar transformation. While attackers employ AI to automate cyberattacks and accelerate vulnerability discovery, defenders are adopting AI to improve threat detection and enhance incident response. Security Operations Centers (SOCs) receive a high volume of alerts from endpoints, cloud workloads, network devices, identity providers, and business applications. Although SIEM and XDR platforms provide visibility into these environments, analysts often spend considerable time correlating alerts, searching documentation, and determining the next investigative steps. AI offers a practical way to augment analysts by providing contextual explanations, summarizing findings, and recommending remediation actions, rather than replacing human expertise. Challenges facing modern SOCs Modern SOCs are expected to detect and respond to sophisticated threats while processing millions of security events every day. High alert volumes contribute to analyst fatigue and increase the likelihood that critical events are overlooked. Investigations frequently require switching between dashboards, documentation, vulnerability databases, and threat intelligence feeds before a complete picture emerges. As infrastructures become increasingly distributed across on-premises and cloud environments, maintaining consistent situational awareness becomes more difficult. AI-assisted workflows help address these challenges by reducing repetitive analysis, adding context, and accelerating investigative decision-making. Organizations can leverage the Wazuh AI Analyst capability on the Wazuh Cloud for guidance on their environment's security posture. Organizations that self-deploy Wazuh can also leverage Wazuh integrations with AI providers. The following sections highlight further details: The Wazuh AI Analyst The Wazuh AI Analyst is automated and hands-off. It is an AI-powered security analysis service for Wazuh Cloud subscriptions that processes your security data through Amazon Bedrock and Anthropic’s Claude, delivering insights without any manual configuration. It periodically emails key indicators, a histogram of protected endpoints, alert volume, active vulnerabilities, and a posture summary with a full PDF report attached. You can also view them from the Wazuh Cloud console in the Environments > AI Reports page. On privacy, subscription data is not shared with third parties and is not used to train AI models; it is processed only to generate your reports, with encrypted transmission, isolated processing, and no permanent storage. As with any AI output, the recommendations are advisory and should be validated against your own policies before you act. Threat hunting and security operations with external AI integrations Beyond the Wazuh AI Analyst, you can expand Wazuh capabilities using a self-hosted LLM and externally managed AI integrations tailored to your needs. Self-hosted Llama 3 and Ollama This integration keeps everything on your own network. Ollama runs the Meta open-source Llama LLM locally on the Wazuh server; a Python script decompresses the archived logs for a chosen period, vectorizes them into a FAISS store, and serves a LangChain-powered chatbot you can query. Nothing is sent to a cloud provider, which makes it well-suited to teams with strict privacy or data-residency requirements. Full setup steps are in the Wazuh blog post: Leveraging artificial intelligence for threat hunting in Wazuh. Externally managed integration with Claude 3.5 Haiku This integration surfaces Anthropic’s Claude 3.5 Haiku, hosted on Amazon Bedrock, as a chat box inside the dashboard through the OpenSearch Assistant. Setup involves enabling the model in Bedrock, installing the relevant OpenSearch plugins, and creating an ML Commons connector, model, and conversational agent. The assistant can provide useful guidance on many common tasks, including what to do about a finding and how to configure certain settings. Full setup steps are in the Wazuh blog post: Leveraging Claude Haiku in the Wazuh dashboard for LLM-powered insights. Conclusion Artificial intelligence is becoming an important capability in modern SOCs. Rather than replacing analysts, it can reduce repetitive work, accelerate investigations, and provide contextual support for detection, triage, and response activities. These capabilities can help security teams operate more efficiently while keeping analysts responsible for validation and consequential decisions. For Wazuh Cloud users, the Wazuh AI Analyst provides automated, scheduled security reports covering key indicators, alert activity, endpoint coverage, active vulnerabilities, and overall security posture. Organizations can further tailor AI-enabled security operations through self-hosted LLM integrations for privacy-sensitive threat hunting or externally managed, cloud-hosted models, aligning adoption with their operational, privacy, and data-residency requirements.

koqjbd.text: Modern phishing campaigns can compromise American businesses without relying on traditional credential theft. Attackers can abuse legitimate cloud services, authentication mechanisms, and trusted business workflows to gain access to corporate accounts while leaving fewer obvious signs behind. ANY.RUN's analysis of Skyw4lker, a device code phishing campaign primarily targeting U.S. organizations, shows how this works in practice. The campaign has focused on manufacturing, technology, and healthcare, using business-themed documents, Google-hosted infrastructure, and Microsoft authentication flows to facilitate account compromise. For security teams, the investigation goes beyond identifying the initial lure. It requires tracing the authentication flow and supporting infrastructure, extracting reliable indicators, and turning those findings into detections that can protect the wider organization. Device Code Phishing: A Growing Challenge for U.S. Organizations The scale of phishing in the United States provides an important backdrop. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center recorded 193,407 phishing and spoofing complaints in 2024, making it one of the most frequently reported categories of internet crime. In 2025, the FBI recorded more than 1 million internet crime complaints and $20.9 billion in reported losses, with reported losses increasing by 26% compared with the previous year. Attackers are also adapting to organizations that have invested heavily in identity security and MFA. Device code phishing is one example. Rather than collecting credentials through a fake login page, an attacker can initiate a legitimate device authorization flow and convince the victim to complete it. The resulting authentication tokens can then provide access to resources available to the compromised account. How Skyw4lker Uses Legitimate Authentication to Compromise Accounts How the Skyw4lker Campaign Works Skyw4lker starts with a lure designed to resemble normal business correspondence, as observed in ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox analysis. The Skyw4lker phishing kit identified in ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox Victims receive a password-protected document presented as a contract or service proposal. The scenario is credible in environments where employees routinely exchange vendor agreements, procurement documents, statements of work, and similar files. From the document, the victim is directed toward a page hosted on sites[.]google[.]com, which eventually leads into a Microsoft authentication flow. Skyw4lker redirecting the victims to a Microsoft365 authentication page The attacker does not need to reproduce Microsoft's login experience perfectly. The authentication itself can be legitimate; the deception is in convincing the victim to complete an authentication request initiated by the attacker. Once the process is completed, the attacker can obtain access to the resulting Microsoft 365 tokens. That makes the attack difficult to evaluate through identity telemetry alone. An organization may see a valid authentication event without immediately seeing the malicious context that caused it. Establishing what happened requires the security team to connect the document, web activity, authentication flow, and associated infrastructure. The Infrastructure Behind the Skyw4lker Phishing Page The web infrastructure used by Skyw4lker provides additional evidence of the campaign's operation. ANY.RUN’s analysis identified obfuscated JavaScript and a PHP backend used to create a victim session, collect information such as IP address and geolocation, and repeatedly poll the backend while waiting for the authentication process to complete. Skyw4lker sample submissions in ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox by country A static inspection of the original document may reveal the starting URL, but it cannot fully explain what happens once the victim interacts with the page. The malicious behavior emerges through the combination of browser activity, JavaScript execution, backend communication, redirects, and authentication. That makes behavioral analysis essential when the objective is to establish exactly what a phishing campaign is doing and which indicators can be trusted for follow-up detection. View the Skyw4lker analysis in ANY.RUN’s Interactive Sandbox to see its complete attack chain and associated IOCs. Reduce Tier 1 workload by up to 20% and give analysts more time to focus on critical threats. Boost Your SOC Efficiency Interactive Sandboxing Turns Suspicious Files and URLs into Actionable Evidence An interactive sandbox lets security teams safely execute and interact with suspicious files, links, and documents, revealing behavior that static inspection can miss. That matters in campaigns such as Skyw4lker, where the document is only the starting point. Analysts need to follow the attack through the browser, observe redirects and authentication activity, inspect network communication, and identify the infrastructure behind the phishing flow. All of this can be done in an isolated ANY.RUN Sandbox environment, with a result available in as little as 40 seconds. The Tier 1 report for the observed Skyw4lker sample available in ANY.RUN’s sandbox Instead of stopping at a malicious/benign verdict, the investigation can produce URLs, domains, IP addresses, network activity, screenshots, behavioral evidence, and other IOCs. These findings give security teams the context needed to validate an alert, scope-related activity, and create detections from evidence gathered during a single investigation. As a result, SOC and MSSP teams can reach a confident verdict faster without manually reproducing the attack across multiple tools, while the resulting intelligence can support threat hunting and detection across the wider environment. Moreover, the same workflow makes it easier for MSSPs to investigate new campaigns and turn findings from one customer case into intelligence that can be searched across other environments. Turning Threat Intel into Earlier Detection The value of an IOC increases when it can be used to detect another attack. ANY.RUN Threat Intelligence Feeds (TI Feeds) provide malicious IPs, domains, URLs, and contextual information derived from sandbox investigations. 99% of unique, high-confidence IOCs are added to TI Feeds after validation, helping security teams work with intelligence that has already been reviewed. ANY.RUN TI Feeds provide live threat intelligence for real-time attack detection ANY.RUN’s internal analysis found that up to 30% of unique malicious IOCs discovered in Interactive Sandbox sessions had already been observed by the company and were present in TI Feeds. When one of these indicators appears in customer telemetry, it can potentially be matched against existing intelligence before an analyst manually investigates the associated sample. This creates a more efficient workflow: known malicious activity can be identified earlier, while sandbox analysis provides the behavioral evidence needed to investigate unfamiliar threats. For internal SOCs, this can reduce time spent researching indicators that are already known to be malicious. For MSSPs, the same intelligence can help identify related activity across multiple customer environments. This is how the existing threat knowledge can be reused instead of reconstructed for every new alert. Cut MTTR by 21 minutes and give your SOC more time to focus on critical threats. Integrate TI Feeds Threat Intelligence Provides Context Behind the Alert An indicator becomes more useful when security teams can understand the activity surrounding it. ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Lookup (TI Lookup) allows analysts to investigate a suspicious domain, IP address, or URL and examine its history and associated activity. In a Skyw4lker-related investigation, this context can help determine whether an indicator is connected to the campaign, has appeared in other malicious activity, or requires further investigation. In addition, ANY.RUN’s Threat Intelligence Reports (TI Reports) provide a broader perspective by connecting indicators with campaigns, infrastructure, techniques, and observed behavior. This can reveal relationships that are difficult to see from individual alerts, such as multiple incidents sharing the same infrastructure or a suspicious domain belonging to a wider phishing operation. When it comes to organizations in U.S. healthcare, manufacturing, and technology, those connections can be especially important. A compromised Microsoft 365 account can expose sensitive communications, intellectual property, operational information, and regulated data, making early identification of related activity critical. How to Make Each SOC and MSSP Investigation More Valuable A successful investigation should improve an organization's ability to detect the next attack. For an MSSP investigating a suspicious contract sent to one American manufacturing customer, indicators associated with Skyw4lker can be searched across other customer environments and incorporated into monitoring. The same approach works within an internal SOC environment, where an IOC found after one employee reports a phishing document can be compared against historical telemetry to identify other potentially affected users. ANY.RUN supports these workflows through API/SDK, STIX/TAXII, SIEM, TIP, and XDR integrations, allowing intelligence from investigations to feed into existing detection and monitoring processes. The result is broader protection from the same investigation: an incident affecting one user can generate intelligence that helps identify related activity across a SOC or MSSP's wider customer base. Uncover up to 58% more threats and gain broader visibility into emerging attacks. Boost Threat Detection Conclusion Skyw4lker shows why modern phishing defense requires visibility beyond the initial lure or login page. By combining interactive sandboxing, threat intelligence, and contextual investigation, security teams can move faster from suspicious artifact to actionable intelligence and broader detection. For organizations in the U.S., that means faster investigations, less repetitive manual work, and a better ability to identify related activity before it becomes a larger incident. The goal is not only to understand one attack, but to turn every investigation into protection against the next one.
